items.descriptionOriginal: Ελπίδα για τα ζευγάρια με ανεξήγητη υπογονιμότητα: σχεδόν τρία στα τέσσερα έγιναν γονείς μέσα σε δύο χρόνια από την έναρξη της θεραπείας, είτε έκαναν εξωσωματική γονιμοποίηση (IVF) είτε ενδομήτρια σπερματέγχυση (IUI). Η εξωσωματική κερδίζει χρόνο, όχι όμως και το τελικό αποτέλεσμα. Σύμφωνα με μελέτη του Πανεπιστημίου του Όκλαντ στη Νέα Ζηλανδία, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο New England Journal of Medicine, οδήγησε γρηγορότερα σε γέννηση, μακροπρόθεσμα όμως οι δύο μέθοδοι είχαν παρόμοια επιτυχία. Η ανεξήγητη υπογονιμότητα, όταν δηλαδή οι εξετάσεις δεν εντοπίζουν καμία προφανή αιτία, αφορά περίπου ένα στα τρία υπογόνιμα ζευγάρια, όπως σημειώνουν οι ερευνητές. Δύο δρόμοι, ένας στόχος Στη δοκιμή FIIX, 585 ζευγάρια από έξι κλινικές γονιμότητας στη Νέα Ζηλανδία χωρίστηκαν τυχαία σε δύο ομάδες. Η μία ξεκίνησε με έως τέσσερις κύκλους σπερματέγχυσης με διέγερση των ωοθηκών και, αν δεν είχε επιτευχθεί εγκυμοσύνη μέσα σε επτά μήνες, μπορούσε να περάσει σε έως δύο κύκλους εξωσωματικής. Η άλλη πήγε κατευθείαν σε έναν ολοκληρωμένο κύκλο εξωσωματικής , με δυνατότητα για έναν ακόμη. Οι γυναίκες ήταν κατά μέσο όρο 34 ετών. Στη σπερματέγχυση , σπέρμα που έχει υποστεί ειδική επεξεργασία τοποθετείται απευθείας στη μήτρα την περίοδο της ωορρηξίας. Στην εξωσωματική , τα ωάρια συλλέγονται, γονιμοποιούνται στο εργαστήριο και, στη συνέχεια, ένα μεταφέρεται στη μήτρα. Η «έκπληξη» της εξωσωματικής Ένας μόνο κύκλος εξωσωματικής οδήγησε σε γέννηση στο 55% των ζευγαριών , έναντι 31% με τέσσερις κύκλους σπερματέγχυσης. « Η εξωσωματική ήταν η έκπληξη », λέει η επικεφαλής συγγραφέας, Δρ Lucy Prentice: το ποσοστό ξεπέρασε τις εκτιμήσεις των ερευνητών, ενώ η σπερματέγχυση απέδωσε όσο αναμενόταν. Στο τέλος της διετίας, ωστόσο, οι δύο ομάδες είχαν τον ίδιο αριθμό μωρών. Όσοι προτιμούν μια πιο αργή και λιγότερο επεμβατική διαδρομή μπορούν, κατά την Δρ Prentice, να ξεκινήσουν με σπερματέγχυση, χωρίς να μειώνουν τις πιθανότητές τους να αποκτήσουν παιδί μέσα σε δύο χρόνια . Η επιλογή, όπως τονίζει, μπορεί να καθοδηγηθεί από τις προτιμήσεις τους. Έως επτά χρόνια μέχρι την πρώτη θεραπεία Η παρούσα μελέτη αφορά ζευγάρια με χαμηλές πιθανότητες φυσικής σύλληψης , που προσπαθούσαν επί χρόνια. Η σπερματέγχυση έγινε με διέγερση των ωοθηκών με κλομιφαίνη, ένα φάρμακο από το στόμα, οπότε τα αποτελέσματα δεν μεταφέρονται απαραίτητα σε άλλα θεραπευτικά πρωτόκολλα. Επιπλέον, η επιτυχία της θεραπείας μειώνεται με την ηλικία, ιδίως μετά τα μέσα της τέταρτης δεκαετίας. Στη Νέα Ζηλανδία, τα ζευγάρια με ανεξήγητη υπογονιμότητα πρέπει να έχουν προσπαθήσει πέντε χρόνια για να διεκδικήσουν δημόσια χρηματοδοτούμενη θεραπεία, και ύστερα να περιμένουν άλλους 12 έως 24 μήνες. Η επικεφαλής ερευνήτρια, καθηγήτρια Cindy Farquhar, ζητά μεγαλύτερη επένδυση στις υπηρεσίες γονιμότητας, υπογραμμίζοντας ότι η χρηματοδότηση έχει μείνει στάσιμη από το 2005. Ελλάδα: Εννέα εξωσωματικές για κάθε σπερματέγχυση Στη χώρα μας σύμφωνα με στοιχεία της Εθνικής Αρχής Ιατρικώς Υποβοηθούμενης Αναπαραγωγής (ΕΑΙΥΑ), το 2023 πραγματοποιήθηκαν 23.083 κύκλοι εξωσωματικής και μόλις 2.672 κύκλοι σπερματέγχυσης . Για το 2024, η Αρχή καταγράφει 21.988 και 2.649 κύκλους αντίστοιχα, χωρίς όμως να έχουν ενσωματωθεί ακόμη τα στοιχεία όλων των μονάδων. Σύμφωνα με τον Ενιαίο Κανονισμό Παροχών Υγείας του ΕΟΠΥΥ, αποζημιώνονται έως τέσσερις ολοκληρωμένες προσπάθειες ιατρικώς υποβοηθούμενης αναπαραγωγής σε ασφαλισμένες έως 50 ετών, με μεσοδιάστημα τουλάχιστον τεσσάρων μηνών, είτε η θεραπεία γίνεται σε δημόσια είτε σε ιδιωτική μονάδα. Διαβάστε επίσης Υπογονιμότητα: Πότε επιλέγεται η σπερματέγχυση και πότε η IVF – Ο ειδικός εξηγεί 10 μύθοι για την εξωσωματική γονιμοποίηση – Τι ισχύει πραγματικά Η ηλικία του πατέρα «δυναμιτίζει» την επιτυχία της εξωσωματικής γονιμοποίησης

items.descriptionOriginal: Μια νέα πυραυλική βάση, στην οποία φιλοξενούνται βαλλιστικοί πύραυλοι στερεών και υγρών καυσίμων, καθώς και πύραυλοι κρουζ , παρουσίασαν οι Φρουροί της Επανάστασης του Ιράν (IRGC), στέλνοντας παράλληλα προειδοποιητικό μήνυμα προς τους αντιπάλους της Τεχεράνης. Σύμφωνα με όσα μετέδωσε την Τρίτη το ιρανικό κρατικό πρακτορείο ειδήσεων IRIB, η νέα εγκατάσταση παρουσιάστηκε από την αεροδιαστημική δύναμη των Φρουρών της Επανάστασης και περιλαμβάνει πυραυλικά συστήματα που έχουν χρησιμοποιηθεί στις πολεμικές συγκρούσεις με το Ισραήλ και τις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες. Το IRIB ανέφερε ότι ορισμένοι από τους πυραύλους χρησιμοποιήθηκαν κατά τη διάρκεια των πολέμων των 12 και 40 ημερών με το Ισραήλ και τις ΗΠΑ. Παράλληλα, υποστήριξε ότι το Ιράν έχει καταργήσει τους περιορισμούς στο βεληνεκές των πυραύλων του , γεγονός που, σύμφωνα με το ιρανικό μέσο, καθιστά τις πολεμικές κεφαλές της χώρας πολύ πιο «καταστροφικές». Ο ισχυρισμός αυτός δεν συνοδεύτηκε από ανεξάρτητα επιβεβαιωμένα τεχνικά στοιχεία. Προειδοποιήσεις από την ηγεσία των ιρανικών ενόπλων δυνάμεων Κατά την τελετή παρουσίασης της νέας βάσης, ο αρχηγός του Γενικού Επιτελείου των ιρανικών ενόπλων δυνάμεων, Αλί Αμπντολαχί, δήλωσε ότι το Ιράν και οι ένοπλες δυνάμεις του λαμβάνουν τις αποφάσεις τους ανεξάρτητα από τη στρατιωτική ισχύ και τους πόρους των αντιπάλων τους, σύμφωνα με το ημιεπίσημο πρακτορείο Fars. Από την πλευρά του, ο διοικητής της αεροδιαστημικής δύναμης των Φρουρών της Επανάστασης, Σεγέντ Ματζίντ Μουσαβί, προειδοποίησε τους αντιπάλους της Τεχεράνης να μην εποφθαλμιούν το Ιράν. Όπως τόνισε, ο ιρανικός λαός θα δώσει απάντηση που θα κάνει τους αντιπάλους του να μετανιώσουν για οποιοδήποτε λάθος τους. Στη σκιά του πολέμου με ΗΠΑ και Ισραήλ Η παρουσίαση της νέας πυραυλικής βάσης πραγματοποιείται σε μια περίοδο έντονης στρατιωτικής αντιπαράθεσης στην περιοχή, μετά τις κοινές επιθέσεις που εξαπέλυσαν οι Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες και το Ισραήλ στις 28 Φεβρουαρίου εναντίον της Τεχεράνης και άλλων ιρανικών πόλεων. Το Ιράν απάντησε με διαδοχικά κύματα επιθέσεων με πυραύλους και μη επανδρωμένα αεροσκάφη, στοχεύοντας το Ισραήλ, καθώς και αμερικανικές στρατιωτικές βάσεις και εγκαταστάσεις στην ευρύτερη περιοχή. Παράλληλα, η Τεχεράνη ενίσχυσε τον έλεγχό της στα Στενά του Ορμούζ. Reuters www.ertnews.gr

items.titleOriginal: 3D-printed polymer hinges cut satellite solar panel deployment weight by 93%
items.description: Ερευνητές στο Ινστιτούτο Fraunhofer της Γερμανίας για την Εφαρμοσμένη Έρευνα Πολυμερών (IAP) ανέπτυξαν μεντεσέδες πολυμερούς με μνήμη σχήματος με 3D εκτύπωση που θα μπορούσαν να βοηθήσουν τους δορυφόρους να αναπτύξουν τους ηλιακούς συλλέκτες τους ενώ φέρουν σημαντικά λιγότερο μηχανικό υλικό. Κάθε μεντεσέ ζυγίζει περίπου 1,4 γραμμάρια, καθιστώντας τον περίπου 93 τοις εκατό ελαφρύτερο από τους συμβατικούς μεντεσέδες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Polymer Research (IAP) have developed 3D-printed shape-memory polymer hinges that could help satellites deploy their solar panels while carrying significantly less mechanical hardware. Each hinge weighs approximately 1.4 grams, making it about 93 percent lighter than conventional hinges currently used in satellite systems, according to the researchers. The components use heat to trigger a programmed shape change, allowing folded solar panels to unfold after launch. The development is part of the Additive Manufacturing of Solar Panels for spACE applications (AM-SPACE) project, which brought together Fraunhofer IAP, German Orbital Systems (GOS), Orion Additive Manufacturing and the Fraunhofer Institute for Reliability and Microintegration IZM. Heat triggers shape recovery The technology uses shape-memory polymers (SMPs), materials that can be programmed into a temporary shape and recover their original form when heated. Researchers processed the polymers into filaments suitable for additive manufacturing and used them to produce hinges and hold-down and release mechanisms (HDRMs). The latter keep satellite components secured during launch before releasing them in a controlled manner once the spacecraft reaches orbit. After the release mechanism activates, the polymer hinges use heat to unfold the solar panels. A heating element raises the hinge’s temperature from 73.4°F to 284°F, triggering its programmed shape recovery. Under controlled laboratory conditions, the hinge completes deployment in about 60 seconds. The approach could reduce the need for conventional mechanical actuation systems, which add weight and complexity to satellite deployment structures. Printing speeds up production The researchers also used additive manufacturing to simplify the production of the components. Printing a hinge or an HDRM takes approximately 15 minutes, followed by another 30 minutes to program its temporary shape. A separate 4D-printing approach integrates the shape-changing response directly into the component during fabrication. Using this method, the team produced HDRMs in approximately five minutes. The researchers say the approach could help satellites launch in a compact configuration before deploying their solar panels or antennas in orbit. It may also enable other activatable components for small spacecraft. Unlike conventional 3D printing, 4D printing incorporates a programmed response that allows a printed object to change shape or function when exposed to an external stimulus , such as heat. The technology has undergone initial laboratory validation, including cleanroom tests, thermal cycling, and preliminary vacuum-chamber experiments. One of the polymers also passed outgassing tests conducted by Spain’s National Institute for Aerospace Technology (INTA). However, the components have not yet been tested in orbit, and their long-term reliability under actual space conditions remains to be established. German Orbital Systems has expressed interest in evaluating the components in space , while discussions are underway for a possible follow-up project aimed at an in-orbit demonstration. The AM-SPACE project ran from October 2023 to September 2026 and received funding through regional innovation programs, with support from the European Union.

items.titleOriginal: Dream Chaser spaceplane hauling 12,000 pounds wins FAA clearance for runway landings
items.description: Η Sierra Space εξασφάλισε μια βασική ρυθμιστική έγκριση για το Dream Chaser, φέρνοντας το διαστημικό αεροπλάνο της που καθυστερούσε πολύ πιο κοντά στην πρώτη του τροχιακή πτήση. Η Ομοσπονδιακή Υπηρεσία Αεροπορίας (FAA) εξουσιοδότησε το διαστημόπλοιο να επιστρέψει από την τροχιά και να προσγειωθεί στη Διαστημική Βάση Δυνάμεων Vandenberg στην Καλιφόρνια. Η εξουσιοδότηση αφορά ένα κρίσιμο μέρος του Dream Chaser.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sierra Space has secured a key regulatory approval for Dream Chaser, bringing its long-delayed spaceplane closer to its first orbital flight. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has authorized the spacecraft to return from orbit and land at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The authorization addresses a critical part of Dream Chaser’s flight operations. Its first mission will launch from Florida aboard United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan Centaur rocket. The spacecraft will then travel back through Earth’s atmosphere before touching down on a conventional runway. Vandenberg becomes primary landing site The FAA issued Dream Chaser’s vehicle operator license on November 9. Sierra Space confirmed the approval the following day. The five-year license permits up to four reentries annually under an unchanged vehicle configuration and mission profile. Vandenberg now serves as the designated landing location for the spacecraft. That represents a change from Sierra Space’s original plans. During an environmental review in 2024, the company identified Kennedy Space Center’s former Space Shuttle runway as its preferred landing site. Another milestone for #DreamChaser ! The @FAANews has issued Sierra Space a license authorizing Dream Chaser to reenter and land at Vandenberg Space Force Base. Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation. pic.twitter.com/qIJgQL54CA — Sierra Space (@SierraSpaceCo) November 10, 2026 Vandenberg initially appeared as a backup option. The newly issued license instead identifies the California installation as Dream Chaser’s landing destination. The arrangement also gives Sierra Space an approved runway for its first flight. However, the FAA authorization does not establish a launch date. Mission timing still depends on the availability of a Vulcan Centaur rocket. Tenacity brings cargo back Dream Chaser’s first spacecraft, Tenacity, combines a lifting-body design with folding wings. The configuration allows it to fit inside Vulcan’s payload fairing during launch. Once in orbit, the spacecraft can carry approximately 12,100 pounds of cargo. Its return capacity reaches 4,080 pounds, according to the FAA’s environmental assessment. That capability addresses an important limitation of conventional cargo spacecraft. Capsules typically return through parachute-assisted landings, often involving ocean recovery. Dream Chaser instead offers a runway landing. Sierra Space says returning cargo experiences less than 1.5 times Earth’s gravity during the journey. The company also claims the spacecraft can use runways designed to accommodate Boeing 737 aircraft. That flexibility could benefit experiments and sensitive equipment requiring careful handling after landing. NASA mission takes new direction Dream Chaser spaceplane originally entered NASA’s commercial resupply program in 2016. Sierra Space secured a contract to develop the spacecraft for International Space Station cargo deliveries. Repeated development delays and propulsion system problems pushed its debut further back. NASA and Sierra Space eventually revised their agreement in September 2025. The revised plan removed the space station docking requirement from Dream Chaser’s initial demonstration. Tenacity will instead conduct an independent free-flying mission in orbit. NASA can still purchase future resupply missions if the demonstration proves successful. Sierra Space has also lined up national security and commercial customers for the inaugural flight. In September, the company confirmed those customers would contribute payloads alongside NASA cargo. However, it has not disclosed their identities or the specific equipment planned for launch. Sierra Space previously targeted late 2026 for the debut mission. The company has tied that schedule to Vulcan Centaur availability. With the year nearing its end, the launch window remains uncertain. The FAA’s approval removes another regulatory hurdle. Tenacity still needs its launch vehicle and remaining mission preparations before its runway return becomes reality.

items.title: Μικροσκοπικός αισθητήρας ραντάρ μετατρέπει τον αντιβράχιο του χρήστη του smartwatch σε trackpad με ακρίβεια 93%
items.titleOriginal: Tiny radar sensor turns smartwatch wearer’s forearm into a trackpad with 93% accuracy
items.description: Ερευνητές στο North Carolina State University ανέπτυξαν μια φορητή τεχνολογία που μετατρέπει το αντιβράχιο σε trackpad, επιτρέποντας στους χρήστες smartwatch να κάνουν κύλιση, ζουμ και κλικ χωρίς να αγγίζουν τη μικροσκοπική οθόνη της συσκευής. Ονομάζεται EpiPad, το σύστημα χρησιμοποιεί έναν συμπαγή αισθητήρα ραντάρ κυμάτων χιλιοστού (mmWave) για την παρακολούθηση των κινήσεων των δακτύλων και τη μέτρηση της σταθερής χρήσης…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a wearable technology that turns the forearm into a trackpad, allowing smartwatch users to scroll, zoom and click without touching the device’s tiny screen. Called EpiPad, the system uses a compact millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar sensor to track finger movements and measure how firmly users press their skin. This enables multi-finger gestures and pressure-sensitive controls similar to those found on laptop trackpads. The researchers say the approach could give smartwatches a larger input surface without increasing their screen size. It could also provide a way to control screenless wearables, including smart glasses. EpiPad’s sensor array measures approximately 5 by 4 millimeters. It is mounted on a wristband and detects the subtle changes in the skin caused when fingertips press against the forearm. Radar tracks finger pressure Unlike conventional touchscreens, EpiPad does not require users to touch a display. Instead, its radar system detects movements and pressure through changes in the signals reflected from the skin. The researchers developed a signal-processing method based on millimeter-wave phase dynamics to estimate applied force. Lightweight machine-learning models then help recognise gestures and interpret the user’s input. Users must first complete a short calibration routine that adapts the system to their individual movements. The process takes 3 minutes and 54 seconds, according to the research paper. The current prototype resembles a wristband with an exposed circuit board. However, the researchers say its components could eventually be integrated into conventional smartwatch designs. Tested across 20 users The team evaluated EpiPad in experiments involving 20 participants. The system achieved 92.8 percent gesture-recognition accuracy and 90.2 percent force-detection accuracy, with a ranging precision of 10.2 millimeters on users who were not included in the training data. In a separate real-time evaluation, participants performed smartwatch input tasks using three methods: a conventional touchscreen , a tilt-based cursor, and EpiPad. The researchers reported that EpiPad outperformed the other two approaches in both error rate and efficiency. The results suggest that using the forearm as an input surface could make small wearable devices easier to control. However, the findings are based on a proof-of-concept prototype and a relatively small user study, rather than a commercially available product. The researchers estimate that the functional components, including the radar sensor array, could cost less than $10. That figure is an estimate from the research team, not the price of a finished device. The technology could eventually extend beyond smartwatches . The researchers suggest that screenless wearables, such as smart glasses, could use the skin as an interactive surface, allowing users to issue commands without relying on a display or physical buttons. The research was detailed in a paper titled “EpiPad: Enabling Multi-Finger and Force-Sensitive Skin Interface for Smartwatches,” published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies . The work was presented at the UbiComp/ISWC 2026 conference in Shanghai.

Η πρώτη γραμμή παραγωγής με το κλειδί στο χέρι έχει προγραμματιστεί να παραδοθεί το πρώτο εξάμηνο του 202…
items.descriptionOriginal: SpaceX has signed a supply deal worth more than $69 million with German equipment maker SINGULUS TECHNOLOGIES to build a production line for high-efficiency heterojunction (HJT) solar cells, securing a manufacturing route for its planned Starmind satellite network. The first turnkey production line is scheduled for delivery in the first half of 2027. It is part of a wider strategic partnership under which SINGULUS plans to supply multiple additional lines as SpaceX accelerates satellite manufacturing at its Bastrop, Texas, facility. SINGULUS disclosed the contract on November 10, saying the partnership will involve developing both high-performance solar cells and the equipment needed to manufacture them. The company said production would scale to support more than 100 gigawatts (GW) of production equipment, although it did not specify the output capacity of the first line. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk subsequently clarified the scale of the order in a post on X, saying the company had ordered 100 GW per year of HJT solar manufacturing equipment from SINGULUS in Germany. He linked the order to Starmind, describing its ambition as creating a “sentient sun.” SpaceX Senior Vice President of Starlink Mike Nicolls said the partnership provides a manufacturing path for solar cells intended for its Starmind satellites. Building cells in-house HJT technology combines a crystalline silicon wafer with thin layers of amorphous silicon. These layers help reduce the loss of electrical charges at the wafer’s surfaces, improving the cell’s ability to convert sunlight into electricity. Manufacturing the cells requires several processes, including wafer cleaning, thin-film deposition, and thermal treatment. SINGULUS develops equipment for these stages, combining wet-chemical processing with vacuum coating technologies such as physical vapor deposition (PVD) and plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD). SpaceX has ordered 100 GW/year of HJT solar manufacturing equipment from Singulus in Germany. This is for Starmind to create a sentient sun. https://t.co/umtNyF9M7g — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 10, 2026 Its production platforms are designed for high-throughput solar cell manufacturing. The company says its equipment supports HJT and other crystalline silicon cell technologies, including TOPCon and interdigitated back-contact designs. The agreement gives SpaceX access to SINGULUS’s manufacturing expertise while establishing a route to produce the cells at its own Texas facility. Neither company has disclosed the planned efficiency of the cells or the production capacity of the initial line. Powering orbital computing SpaceX’s Starmind program centers on satellites carrying computing payloads that use solar energy generated in orbit. The company’s published specifications for its AI1 satellite describe a deployed height of 30 meters, a wingspan of 75 meters, and a computing payload drawing up to 250 kilowatts at peak and 175 kilowatts on average. The satellites are designed to operate in sun-synchronous orbit and transmit data to the ground through laser links connected to the Starlink network, according to SpaceX. The scale of the planned network is substantial. In its 2026 securities filing, SpaceX outlined a long-term ambition to deploy up to 100 GW of power to orbit annually. The company said reaching that level would require thousands of launches each year, while noting that it could build a commercially viable business at considerably lower deployment rates. SINGULUS said its strategic partnership with SpaceX began in March 2026. SpaceX provided significant funding to the German company that month and again in October through a subordinated secured loan. The first production line is expected in the first half of 2027, as SpaceX prepares to expand satellite manufacturing in Texas.

items.descriptionOriginal: The year I turned 30, I moved to a peaceful neighborhood on Los Angeles’ Westside. I was 10 minutes from Venice Beach and had an apartment all to myself. The only catch (besides street parking)? It was 450 square feet. A couple of friends helped me optimize the place: We assembled a custom Murphy bed, installed a wall-mounted folding table, and chose decor that made it feel joyful and airy. Though I lamented not having more space at times, I discovered that my scaled-down quarters came with some perks. Styling the studio so intentionally felt empowering, and because it was so small, I often enjoyed my meals out in the courtyard under the sun. Years later, despite having married and moved into a comfortable condo, I still occasionally yearn for more square footage, particularly during dinner parties or when family visits for the holidays. To refresh my perspective, I spoke to interior design experts and therapists who helped illuminate some of the unexpected benefits of having a smaller home — and offered tips for making the most of yours. Benefits domin_domin—iStock/Getty Images Plus Cost and Cleaning We’ll start with perhaps the most obvious but still occasionally overlooked perks: “Less square footage means less time cleaning and organizing. Owning less means spending less time managing and maintaining your belongings,” Phoenix-based interior designer Mackenzie Collier explained in an email to Nice News. “That frees up more time for hobbies, socializing, and anything else you’d rather be doing!” She added that smaller spaces force us to be more thoughtful about what we buy and why (a welcome mindset shift for many), and that the money we save on quantity can be used to invest in quality — e.g., well-built furniture, bespoke decor, art. And it’s not just our shopping carts that feel the difference, Sierra Troitsky , an interior designer in Indianapolis, pointed out. “Smaller spaces are often more economical and environmentally friendly as they cost less to heat and cool,” she said. Mental Well-Being Less square footage can contribute to a greater sense of well-being because it can encourage us to be neat and organized, “which is calming for the brain,” said Sipora Weissman , a licensed therapist in Ventura, California. In a tiny room, a pile of unfolded laundry is a lot more noticeable than in a large one, for example, so we may be more inclined to actually, you know, put it away . “As a therapist who works with adults who get overstimulated easily, living in a small space can be overwhelming or it can actually be very supportive to someone’s nervous system,” Weissman explained. “If you fill that small space with tchotchkes and clutter, that will be a recipe for an unsettled brain. There are many scientific studies that show the negative impacts of clutter on the brain. But if you take this small space living situation as an opportunity, it can be very conducive to your mental health.” More Intentional Decor Just as I experienced when decorating my tiny quarters, less to work with can have a focusing effect. “A small living room lends itself to intentional decorating because you’re forced to narrow in on fewer, impactful pieces that set the tone for the space — say, a beautiful sofa, a well-sized rug, task and accent lighting, and some meaningful artwork,” said Elena Navarro, an interior designer and professional organizer at Sparkly Maid Austin . View this post on Instagram She added: “I love that limited square footage forces you to really think through everything that you bring in the door, from new dishes to cozy throw blankets to holiday decor. Where is the item going to live? Do you use it enough to warrant giving it a permanent home?” Better for Gathering and Bonding The reason celebrity chef Ina Garten considers six people the ideal number for a dinner party is the same reason your modest home might lend itself to more meaningful gatherings: intimacy. “Small group events tend to produce an environment that allows for more personalized conversation,” explained Whitney Willborn , a Texas-based licensed clinical social worker, adding that it’s easier to not only include everyone in the conversation but also to spot when others appear to be excluded. If guests are spread out in different rooms or fragmented into groups, it’s trickier to notice when a new friend is standing awkwardly by themself, for example. Your own family might benefit from a smaller floor plan, too. Collier recently moved out of a 900-square-foot home, and her household has experienced some nostalgia for the cozier living situation. “There was nowhere to escape to, so we’d sit together, watch a movie, or play games,” she said. “Those shared moments became some of our favorite memories.” Spend More Time in Community My al fresco dining habit of yore highlights how the wide world can beckon when your indoors isn’t vast. Collier had the same experience. “I’ve found that living in a small space encourages me to spend more time outdoors and in my community,” she shared. “Whether it was tending to my garden, or heading to a local coffee shop to work, living small naturally pushed me to get out into the community more.” Tips Double Duty Interior designer Preeti Shah made her name in New York, where minuscule apartments are no big deal (one of the tiniest is an infinitesimal 55 square feet !). When she moved to an area of Houston filled with massive homes, she was bemused. At around 3,000 square feet, her house is among the smallest — yet she said it’s where her neighborhood pals prefer to hang out. Courtesy of Preeti Shah Shah’s lounge area with convertible coffee-to-dining room table A design principle Shah prioritizes, in any sized space, is double duty. “Anything I purchase, I would like for my client to be able to use it in more than just one way,” she shared. Ottomans are great for seating and storage, twin beds can become kings when guests stay over, and dining chairs should be comfy enough to be used as additional living room seating. In her own house, rather than a dining room table that sits unused, she opted for a convertible coffee table that lifts and extends to seat 10. Size and Amount Matter Troitsky explained that getting furniture that’s sized correctly can help a lot with how large your home feels (e.g., an enormous couch in a tiny bedroom might make the space seem small). But that doesn’t mean you should automatically purchase miniature versions of everything you’d buy for a bigger area. “It’s best to take inventory of what you actually use, need, and love, and start there,” Navarro said. She added: “For holiday decor, instead of trying to deck out every inch of your small living space, pick one or two areas to really lean into — the Christmas tree, the mantel, the coffee table, etc.” Get Comfortable With Borrowing Why use up valuable storage space on extra glassware and guest seating for your one annual holiday get-together when you can call a friend and ask to borrow theirs? As a bonus, it gives you both an excuse for a visit. Another option is to rent what you need when you need it. Ultimately, do your best to remember that, as Navarro put it, “the goal is always to make your guests feel at home — not to impress them with how big your place is!” RELATED: Make Your Home Happier With These Dopamine-Inducing Decorating Tips

Τον Μάρτιο του 2020, τα lockdowns COVID έκλεισαν τα σχολεία σε όλο τον κόσμο, συμπεριλαμβανομένου του καταυλισμού προσφύγων Tongogara στη Ζιμπάμπουε, όπου ο πρίγκιπας Μπασανγκέζι ολοκλήρωνε τις σπουδές του σε Α-Επίπεδο. Το στρατόπεδο βρίσκεται κοντά στο t…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. In March 2020, COVID lockdowns shuttered schools around the world, including at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, where Prince Bashangezi was completing his A-Level studies. The camp sits near the Mozambique border, home to more than 17,000 people displaced by conflict across central and eastern Africa. Formal schooling stopped. Prince and a group of fellow A-Level students at USAP Community School, a school serving refugee youth in the camp, decided not to wait for it to resume. They founded TWEENS : Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. The model was built around what they had: each other. Teaching from inside the camp TWEENS began as a service learning project, with refugee students tutoring younger students in the same camp. The premise was direct. These were students who understood exactly what it meant to study without resources, without stability , often without continuous access to teachers, and in many cases without families to support them. They knew the particular difficulty of trying to build a future from inside a displaced population. So they taught each other. The program was supported by Education Matters Africa , a Zimbabwe-based nonprofit, and launched at a moment when any alternative to organized education was better than none. What began during a global lockdown became something that outlasted it. Prince was also a Waterford Kamhlaba UWC of Southern Africa alumnus, a school known for selecting students across conflict zones and economic hardship who show unusual potential and commitment. That network eventually connected him to the Global Student Haven Initiative at Pomona College in California, where he now studies computer science and economics. Marianne Langridge, who nominated Prince for this series, wrote that he “has turned his personal tragedy of losing his family during war into loving service for others.” That framing, loss converted into something that benefits others, runs through how Prince has talked about his work and what TWEENS is for. Langridge described his commitment as rooted in wanting students in refugee camps to “gain access to education so they can have hope for a better future.” Why peer tutoring works here There is something specific about a peer model in a refugee context that a standard school or aid program can’t replicate. The tutors in TWEENS are not professionals, not volunteers flying in from outside, not people working from a comfortable distance. They are students who live where the students they’re teaching live. They went through the same disruptions. Their credibility comes from proximity, not credentials. This is similar in structure to the peer-learning model that makes other youth-run programs effective, but in a refugee camp the stakes of educational continuity are different. A child who falls significantly behind in a displacement context faces a compounding disadvantage. Keeping any educational thread alive, even an informal one built by A-Level students during a lockdown, matters more than it might in a setting with backup resources. TWEENS was built on that understanding. From Tongogara to Pomona Prince arrived at Pomona College through the Global Student Haven Initiative , which supports students from refugee and displaced communities. He is studying computer science and economics, a combination that maps directly to the problems TWEENS is trying to solve: how technology and resource allocation interact to either expand or cut off access to education. Pomona profiled him in 2024 as part of a piece on Global Haven students finding opportunity in higher education. A fundraising campaign on GlobalGiving continues to support TWEENS’ operations, keeping the peer tutoring program funded as he completes his degree. What Prince Bashangezi and his fellow students built during a lockdown in a refugee camp, with nothing but time and knowledge and the willingness to share both, is still running more than five years later. TWEENS now offers an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside its original peer tutoring. To support TWEENS, visit their GlobalGiving fundraising page . The post Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The question hanging over international climate talks for years has not really been whether the world would shift away from fossil fuels. It has been whether the countries most responsible for burning them would actually put that transition in writing, with a plan attached. On November 3, Brazil did exactly that, releasing what it calls the world’s first global roadmap for phasing out coal, oil and gas. The document doesn’t bind anyone. It’s voluntary, and it acknowledges upfront that countries will move at different speeds and need different kinds of support. It names the transition as “urgent, inevitable and yet possible” and lays out a three-phase agenda running from 2028 to 2033, during which countries are urged to start drawing up plans and transforming their energy systems. “Countries differ in how fast they can move and in the support they need,” it states, “but every country gains from immediately planning its transition away from fossil fuels.” Why COP30 ended without naming fossil fuels The COP30 climate summit, held earlier this year in Belém, ended without final text that explicitly named fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia, and other major oil producers pushed back against direct language. Fortunately, the Brazilian presidency didn’t treat that as a dead end. Instead, it spent the remaining months of its COP30 term putting together a voluntary framework that any country can use to plan its own phaseout, entirely separate from whatever gets negotiated at a formal summit. COP30 chief executive Ana Toni framed the roadmap in terms of self-interest as much as obligation. “The transition is inevitable, so start planning now and as soon as possible, because this will be good for your country, for your society, for your economy,” she said. Brazil also released a companion roadmap on halting deforestation by 2030. A three-phase transition plan, tailored by country The roadmap doesn’t tell anyone exactly what to do. It says outright that “there is no unique solution for this complex puzzle” and pushes countries to tailor their approach to their own circumstances and starting points. The framing throughout is that the transition is a logistics problem, something to start working on with tools and knowledge that already exist, not a debate to be settled at some future summit. COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago was blunt about it: “Everyone can start to act now. The agreements already exist. What’s important is to implement them.” The document also points out that current policies still leave the world short of the commitments made at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, when nearly 200 nations agreed to language about “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems.” Three years later, that language hasn’t moved much. The roadmap is an attempt to change that without waiting on another round of negotiations to get there. The roadmap’s role at COP31 in Antalya The COP31 conference opened in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9 with the roadmap on the agenda, though Brazil has been clear it’s not there for renegotiation. “We are not suggesting negotiations,” Corrêa do Lago said. It’s a standing offer. Turkey and Australia, which are co-steering this year’s talks, have put electrification at the center of COP31’s agenda as a path to cutting emissions. The concern critics have raised is a practical one: the draft text doesn’t specify clean sources, which leaves open the possibility that “electrification” gets used to describe fossil fuel expansion rather than a genuine move to renewables. How that plays out over the two weeks in Antalya will shape what the summit actually delivers. Climate advocates are pushing for specificity. “The roadmap must not end up as just another report gathering dust on a shelf,” said Fanny Petitbon, a policy analyst at 350.org. “COP31 must be the moment when governments take this work forward, with clear commitments, timelines and the resources to deliver a fair and orderly exit from coal, oil and gas.” The framing shift that may outlast any summit The roadmap has no legal teeth. However, what it does have is a particular assumption baked in, namely that the question isn’t whether the fossil fuel transition happens, but how. That’s a different starting point than the one that has dominated climate negotiations for most of the past decade, where the fight was still about whether countries would formally commit to leaving fossil fuels behind at all. Brazil’s document takes that commitment as a given and asks what planning for it looks like. Whether the summits that follow treat it that way remains to be seen, but the document is in the world now, and that changes what any country can point to when it decides to start. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Fox, ο οποίος έχει κυρίως Πάρκινσο…
items.descriptionOriginal: The Apple series Shrinking centers around actor Jason Segel, who plays a therapist juggling grief, fatherhood, and experimenting with unconventional therapy practices with his patients. It also stars Harrison Ford , who plays Segel’s mentor and boss, a therapist who is living with Parkinson’s disease. Actor Michael J. Fox , who notably has Parkinson’s in real life, was so moved by Ford’s “human” and “accessible” portrayal of the condition that he called up Bill Lawrence, his former Spin City boss, who also co-created Shrinking . And, as he shared in an interview with the LA Times , Fox didn’t mince words: “Bill, why the f*** am I not on the show?” Truly, only Fox could deliver such a line in a way that immediately feels charming and friendly. Pretty soon, plans were set in motion to have Fox guest star, marking his first return to acting since 2020 . The pairing nobody expected to see In the Season 3 premiere, which aired on January 28 , Ford’s character comes in for a doctor’s visit. While waiting to be seen, he encounters a fellow patient with Parkinson’s, played by Fox. It’s clear that Fox’s character will serve as a mentor and friend throughout the season. As to be expected, the Back to the Future star does not fall short on comedic expectations. For instance, during the scene (which you can see in the video above), Fox asks Ford what he’s in for. Ford responds, “Parkinson’s. You?” Without missing a beat, Fox replies, “Just a haircut.” He follows with the quip, “I fall three times a day. I’m thinking of taking up stunt work.” Why the whole cast was buzzing Castmates instantly knew that seeing two icons, Marty McFly and Indiana Jones, acting together for the first time was something special. As Shrinking co-star Michael Urie noted, “Everyone’s hearts grew” in anticipation and nostalgia once Fox showed up to set. How the scene hit Fox the hardest But perhaps no one was more affected than Fox himself. Speaking with Vanity Fair, he shared, “I wasn’t prepared for how much of [Ford’s] own understanding of the disease he brought to it. I mean, I recognized Parkinson’s in his eyes. The things I was feeling, I recognized in the way he was expressing himself.” It was such a powerful performance that Fox told the outlet, “I was just brought to tears by it.” “I should say he’s an underrated actor because everybody knows how great he is, but the subtlety of his work, so brilliant and so fun to work with,” Fox continued. Ford’s sentiment, it seems, was the same. In the same interview, he called Fox “an extraordinarily powerful person.” Shrinking is streaming on Apple TV , and the show has been renewed for a fourth season. This article originally appeared in February. It has been updated. The post Michael J. Fox saw Harrison Ford’s Parkinson’s acting on ‘Shrinking,’ and immediately reached out appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Η ποικιλομορφία της ανθρωπότητας σημαίνει ότι οι άνθρωποι δεν θα βλέπουν πάντα τα μάτια με τα μάτια και η ψυχολογία μας λέει ότι οι άνθρωποι τείνουν να διπλασιάζονται όταν αμφισβητούνται οι απόψεις τους. Όταν οι άνθρωποι είναι τόσο βαθιά ριζωμένοι στις δικές τους προοπτικές που αρνούνται να διασκεδάσουν άλλες απόψεις, τι κάνουμε; Συχνά, αυτό που κάνουμε εμπίπτει στο «κατανοητό αλλά αναποτελεσματικό…
items.descriptionOriginal: The diversity of humanity means people won’t always see eye to eye , and psychology tells us that people tend to double down when their views are challenged . When people are so deeply entrenched in their own perspectives that they refuse to entertain other viewpoints, what do we do? Frequently, what we do falls into the “understandable but ineffective” category. When we disagree with someone because their opinion is based on falsehoods or inaccurate information, we may try to pound them with facts and statistics. Unfortunately, research shows that generally doesn’t work . We might try to find different ways to explain our stance using logic and reasoning, but that rarely makes a dent, either. So often, we’re left wondering how on Earth this person arrived at their perspective, especially if they reject facts and logic. According to Stanford researchers, turning that wondering into an actual question might be the key. Questions are more effective than facts when it comes to disagreements. Photo credit: Canva The power of “Tell me more” Two studies examined how expressing interest in someone’s view and asking them to elaborate on why they hold their opinion affected people on both sides of a disagreement. They found that asking questions like, “Could you tell me more about that?” and “Why do you think that?” made the other person “view their debate counterpart more positively, behave more open-mindedly, and form more favorable inferences about other proponents of the counterpart’s views.” Additionally, adding an expression of interest, such as, ‘“But I was interested in what you’re saying. Can you tell me more about how come you think that?” not only made the counterpart more open to other viewpoints, but the questioner themselves developed more favorable attitudes toward the opposing viewpoint. In other words, genuinely striving to understand another person’s perspective by being curious and asking them to say more about how they came to their conclusions may help bridge seemingly insurmountable divides. Stanford isn’t alone in these findings. A series of studies at the University of Haifa also found that high-quality listening helped lower people’s prejudices, and that when people perceive a listener to be responsive, they tend to be more open-minded. Additionally, the perception that their attitude is the correct and valid one is reduced. Why curiosity works In some sense, these results may seem counterintuitive. We may assume that asking someone to elaborate on what they believe and why they believe it might just further entrench them in their views and opinions. But that’s not what the research shows. Dartmouth cognitive scientist Thalia Wheatley studies the role of curiosity in relationships and has found that being curious can help create consensus where there wasn’t any before. “[Curiosity] really creates common ground across brains, just by virtue of having the intellectual humility to say, ‘OK, I thought it was like this, but what do you think?’ And being willing to change your mind,” she said, according to the John Templeton Foundation . Asking people to elaborate leads to more open-mindedness. Photo credit: Canva Of course, there may be certain opinions and perspectives that are too abhorrent or inhumane to entertain with curious questions, so it’s not like “tell me more” is always the solution to an intractable divide. But even those with whom we vehemently disagree or those whose views we find offensive may respond to curiosity with more open-mindedness and willingness to change their view than if we simply argue with them. And isn’t that the whole point? How to actually put this into practice Sometimes what’s effective doesn’t always line up with our emotional reactions to a disagreement, so engaging with curiosity might take some practice. It may also require us to rethink what formats for public discourse are the most impactful. Is ranting in a TikTok video or a tweet conducive to this shift in how we engage others? Is one-on-one or small group, in-person discussion a better forum for curious engagement? These are important things to consider if our goal is not to merely state our case and make our voice heard but to actually help open people’s minds and remain open-minded in our own lives as well. This article originally appeared in February. It has been updated. The post Stanford researchers find a single question could be the key to changing someone’s mind appeared first on Upworthy .

Καθώς εναποτίθενται οργανικά στρώματα, τα μόριά τους μπορούν να ευθυγραμμιστούν για να δημιουργήσουν ένα εσωτερικό ηλεκτρικό δυναμικό γνωστό ως γιγαντιαίο δυναμικό επιφάνειας (GSP). Όταν αυτό το δυναμικό αντλεί υπερβολικά θετικά φορτία, ή τρύπες, κοντά στο λι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) power many display screens, but their efficiency can be limited by energy lost inside the device. As organic layers are deposited, their molecules can align to create an internal electrical potential known as giant surface potential (GSP). When this potential draws excess positive charges, or holes, near the light-emitting layer, they can interfere with light-producing excitons. This process, called exciton–polaron quenching, reduces emitted light and can affect device performance.

items.description: Η καλύτερη φωτογραφία σας κάνει να επιβραδύνετε και να παρατηρήσετε κάτι που διαφορετικά θα μπορούσε να αγνοηθεί — και οι φιναλίστ για την όγδοη έκδοση του Close-Up Photographer of the Year κάνουν ακριβώς αυτό. Οι εικόνες που προκρίθηκαν μόλις αποκαλύφθηκαν από ένα ρεκόρ 15.388 υποβολών σε 11 κατηγορίες. Το παραπάνω πλάνο, με τίτλο «Χρυσή σκόνη», είναι ένα από τα επίμαχα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The best photography makes you slow down and notice something that might otherwise go overlooked — and the finalists for the eighth edition of Close-Up Photographer of the Year do just that. The shortlisted images were just revealed out of a record 15,388 submissions across 11 categories. The above shot, titled “Golden dust,” is one of the contenders in the animals category and features a Eurasian hoopoe taking a dust bath outside of Aurangabad, India. The dust helps remove excess oil from the bird’s feathers so they don’t stick together, but according to photographer Sarthak Agrawal, the swirling particles also make a good shot “especially difficult” (and thus especially impressive). “This year’s shortlist is a fabulous showcase of imagination, technical expertise, and natural curiosity,” competition co-founder Tracy Calder said in a press release shared with Nice News. The top 100 pics and the winning photographers will be announced in January, but submissions aren’t closed just yet. The competition holds an adjacent challenge that follows a specific theme, and this year’s is “Close to Home.” Hopeful shutterbugs of any age and skill level have until Nov. 30 to enter and Dec. 7 to upload their pics to the website. “Proving you don’t have to travel far to find something extraordinary,” the website states about the theme choice, which was voted on by the public. “We’re looking for close-up, macro, and micro photographs taken in a home and its immediate surroundings: the home’s rooms, outbuildings (such as sheds, garages, and greenhouses), garden, balcony, doorstep, or the street directly outside. This may be your own home or the home of family or friends.” Scroll to view a selection of the shortlisted images. Studio Art: “Rose Thorns” by Donald Bolak © Donald Bolak/CUPOTY “Fairly high level of magnification for a macro shot of a single rose thorn. The larger thorn is about 3/8 inch high. This is one of the things I enjoy most about macro — discovering sights unseen and unimagined. In this case a slightly surreal and alien landscape where rose thorns can be mountain peaks.” Young: “A Little Punky” by Oliver Lacey © Oliver Lacey/CUPOTY “I photographed this male Green Jumping Spider (Mopsus mormon) with its characteristic (and rather impressive) mohawk hairstyle in my suburban backyard in Brisbane, Australia.” Invertebrate Portrait: “Isopod portrait” by Adam Ferry © Adam Ferry/CUPOTY “I found this woodlouse resting underneath a piece of bark in a local woodland in Surrey, England. As it was fairly cold the woodlouse remained perfectly still allowing me to capture this focus stack of 80 photos. I love the high level of detail I could due to the increased magnification as the portrait filled most of the frame.” Underwater: “Rockpool Sanctuary” by Lisa Skelton © Lisa Skelton/CUPOTY “Young elephant seal pups or ‘weaners’ gather around natural rock pools on the Falkland Islands, using the protected waters to practice swimming and diving until they are ready to venture out to sea.” Intimate Landscape: “Where Worlds Collide” by Johannes Kowalewski © Johannes Kowalewski/CUPOTY “High above the Baltic Sea, an ancient beech forest glows in autumn colorrs atop the dramatic white chalk cliffs of Jasmund National Park on the island of Rügen, Germany.” Animals: “Nosepick” by Steffen Foerster © Steffen Foerster/CUPOTY “A blackish cinclodes or tussock-bird (Cinclodes antarcticus) picks at the nose of a resting southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) on Sea Lion Island, in the Falkland Islands.” Insects: “Spoonwing” by Lucien Harris © Lucien Harris/CUPOTY “I followed this spoonwing for over 10 minutes as it clumsily flew along the border of an overgrown field in the Peloponnese region of Greece, waiting for the perfect backdrop to compose a photo of this beautiful creature.” Underwater: “Fish Out of Context” by Marco Domenicucci © Marco Domenicucci/CUPOTY “A shoal of goldfish swim in an urban pond inside a metropolitan business district. Two worlds divided by a thin waterline: glass and concrete above and an aquatic ecosystem below.” Young: “Fight for the Perfect Fishing Spot” by Sasha Jumanca © Sasha Jumanca/CUPOTY “I managed to photograph these two blue kingfishers in December while they were defending their fishing territory in Schlosspark Nymphenburger, Munich. They faced each other directly and even tried to push one another under the water, showing how they compete for the best spots. This kind of behavior is quite rare, as kingfishers usually defend their territory by calling or chasing each other, rather than through physical contact.” Intimate Landscape: “Untitled 14” by Lukas Furlan © Lukas Furlan/CUPOTY “I was already fascinated by this scene, but rotating the image later revealed an entirely different world, almost like looking through a portal. It’s a reminder of the magic of experimentation and unexpected discoveries in photography.” Animals: “Suspended” by Joao Pontes © Joao Pontes/CUPOTY “In Portugal, there is no reptile quite as remarkable as the chameleon. Every year, towards the end of summer, the Algarve fills with juvenile chameleons. Naturally discreet, they become more active as the sun climbs higher in the sky, setting off to explore the world around them. Here, at the edge of the ocean, they inhabit the coastal dunes. At their scale, the slender stems of sea pinks become towering lianas, suspended pathways through this sandy jungle. To capture this image, I used a fisheye lens, aiming for a composition that would reveal not only the chameleon itself, but also the perhaps unexpected habitat it calls home.”

Hanlon, έναν Αμερικανό συγγραφέα. Είναι αυτό:…
items.descriptionOriginal: It sometimes feels impossible not to take things personally . But what if statistics proved that most experiences are not, indeed, personal? That what we chalk up to an attack on our character could actually just be forgetfulness or self-centeredness? The concept is called Hanlon’s Razor , coined by Robert J. Hanlon, an American writer. It’s this: “Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity.” Of course, this can’t explain every interaction, as obviously some things are unfortunately done with personal and/or malicious intent. But there are many times, it’s simply not the case. View this post on Instagram Britannica.com describes the idea as a “heuristic reasoning tool,” meaning it’s quick and helpful, if not exactly science-based. The explanation continues, “The statement is a reminder to give others the benefit of the doubt by considering alternative explanations for their actions rather than assuming that they intend harm. For example, if someone does not receive a response from their close friend after sending their friend a text, that person might assume that their friend is upset with them and intentionally not responding. In reality, the friend’s cell phone battery may have died, and the friend might not have had time to recharge it.” This can be used in situations spanning all parts of life. Here are a few: The workplace In the article “Why More Employees Should Learn Hanlon’s Razor” for Forbes , Jamie Flinchbaugh first softens the original wording. “‘Stupid’ sounds pretty harsh, so let’s break that term down into more accurate and compassionate terms, especially in terms of workplace decisions. Two key components are naivety and ignorance.” Flinchbaugh shares the example of a boss assigning a task. “You’re massively overloaded and your boss comes to you with a new big project. Most employees will take the project and then grumble to someone about how inconsiderate their boss is. If you instead assume ignorance, you can show your boss your current to-do list and ask where the new task should fall on that list of priorities. With this new information, your boss may rethink that assignment or let you know you can de-prioritize other work.” Should the issue be naivety, there are ways to tackle that, as well. “Outline the steps or methods you might use, and ask for recommendations for how to complete it more effectively or efficiently. This will force them to look behind the request and engage with how the work might get completed.” Romantic relationships In an article for Tech Tello, Vinita Bansal uses this tool for all relationships, noting times when it seems a partner “might not have your best intentions at heart.” She writes, “In these moments, applying Hanlon’s razor can enable you to shift from assuming bad intentions to exploring other alternative viewpoints. It may strengthen your relationship as you approach the other person with the desire to understand instead of blame.” Bansal adds, “The major German literary figure Johann Wolfgang von Goethe published ‘The Sorrows of Young Werther’, in which he stated ‘Misunderstandings and neglect create more confusion in this world than trickery and malice. At any rate, the last two are certainly much less frequent.’ Opening your mind to seek other views shifts your perspective from a negative frame of mind to a positive one, from shutting down communication to actively engaging and blaming others to finding solutions together.” Friendships In a clip posted to social media, Raleigh Williams discusses the concept with his preteen daughter. He notes in the chyron that this is in fact the “most common fallacy with preteens.” View this post on Instagram He says to his daughter, “You were telling me you think your friends are being mean for not inviting you to hang out. What fallacy is that?” She answers, “Hanlon’s Razor. Whenever you assume that someone is just trying to be cruel, they could just be forgetful.” Williams turns to the camera and reiterates the idea. “Never assume maliciousness when forgetfulness or stupidity is more likely an explanation.” With over 130,000 likes on Instagram/ Facebook , well over 1,000 people chimed in on the conversation. While some advised being leery of “smart people pretending to be naïve,” many praised the wisdom. One Facebooker writes, “If more parents taught their kids logical fallacies, this world would be a utopia.” The post Experts explain 3 ways to apply ‘Hanlon’s Razor’ in everyday life. It might be a game-changer. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι αρχαιολόγοι έσπασαν τον κωδικό σε μια κλειδαριά 400 ετών που βρέθηκε στο ναυάγιο του Ann Francis
items.titleOriginal: Archaeologists cracked the code on a 400-year-old lock found in the Ann Francis shipwreck
items.description: Στις 28 Δεκεμβρίου 1583, το Ann Francis, ένα ελισαβετιανό εμπορικό πλοίο, πήγαινε στο σπίτι του προς το Νόρφολκ της Αγγλίας, από την Ισπανία όταν μια ισχυρή καταιγίδα το οδήγησε στην παραλία Margam στην Ουαλία, πάνω από 250 μίλια, καθώς το κοράκι πετάει, από τον προορισμό του. Το Ann Francis είχε παραδώσει ένα φορτίο σιταριού στην Ισπανία και επέστρεψε με χρυσό και ασήμι χρυσό. Είναι beli…
items.descriptionOriginal: On December 28, 1583, the Ann Francis , an Elizabethan merchant ship, was on its way home to Norfolk, England, from Spain when a powerful storm drove it onto Margam beach in Wales, over 250 miles, as the crow flies , from its destination. The Ann Francis had delivered a shipment of wheat to Spain and returned with gold and silver bullion. It’s believed that around 14 sailors died on the wreck, and the ship became a target for local looters, but they didn’t get everything. For centuries, the ship’s cargo lay on the sandy ocean floor until metal detectorist Peter Hughes uncovered it between 1996 and 2017. One of his most mysterious finds was a combination lock. The northern side of Sker Point, near where the Ann Francis was wrecked. Credit: Wikimnedia Commons The lock was in incredible condition for its age “When I found the lock, I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition,” Hughes told Amgueddfa Cymru , or Museum Wales, in English. “When I moved the ring dials of the combination, they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands, and I was left in disbelief. I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked.” The researchers found the lock near Spanish silver coins and two coin weights near the wreck site. The lock may have secured a chest holding the coins or other valuable items lost to the sea, such as textiles or important documents. Coins and a lock found at the Ann Francis wreck site. Credit: Amgueddfa Cymru (press release) They examined the lock with a CT scan The researchers wanted to open the combination lock to understand how it was manufactured and learn the secret code that last locked it 443 years ago. To examine the lock without destroying any of its ancient components, researchers used a CT scan. “Micro-CT scanning allowed us to look inside the lock without damaging it. By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination,” Dr. David Williams , a research associate based at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University’s School of Engineering, explained. “We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us! I had to wait until later that evening for the museum team to test the combination, so getting the message that we’d cracked it was incredibly satisfying,” Williams continued. “It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!” After careful analysis, the researchers found the combination was ANCE. But what does the combination mean? Modern CT scanner located at the Lochotín University Hospital in Pilsen, Czech Republic. Credit: Wikimedia Commons “Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve,” Alastair Willis, Senior Curator for Numismatics and the Welsh Economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in a statement. “Of course, now we’ve solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner.” One of the great joys of archaeology is that the mysteries can go on forever, like pulling a thread from a sweater. The researchers used a brilliant means to discover the secret code, and now they face an even larger, more existential question: What does it all mean? (If anything.) The post Archaeologists cracked the code on a 400-year-old lock found in the Ann Francis shipwreck appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Φοιτητής αρχαιολογίας βρήκε μια χαμένη πόλη των Μάγια στη σελίδα 16 μιας αναζήτησης στο Google
items.titleOriginal: Archaeology student found a lost Maya city on page 16 of a Google search
items.description: Οι περισσότερες μεγάλες αρχαιολογικές ανακαλύψεις περιλαμβάνουν χρόνια επιτόπιας εργασίας, πυκνή ζούγκλα και πολλές ανασκαφές. Αυτό περιλάμβανε έναν τύπο που έκανε κλικ στις σελίδες των αποτελεσμάτων της Google, το είδος της κουνελότρυπας στο Διαδίκτυο που οι περισσότεροι από εμάς πέφτουμε μόνο όταν βαριόμαστε στο σπίτι . Ο Luke Auld-Thomas, τότε διδάκτορας στο Πανεπιστήμιο Tulane, ήταν βαθιά σε μια αναζήτηση όταν…
items.descriptionOriginal: Most great archaeological discoveries involve years of fieldwork, dense jungle, and a lot of digging. This one involved a guy clicking through page after page of Google results, the kind of Internet rabbit hole most of us only tumble into when we’re bored at home . Luke Auld-Thomas, then a PhD student at Tulane University, was deep in a search when he found it. “I was on something like page 16 of Google search and found a laser survey done by a Mexican organization for environmental monitoring,” he told the BBC in 2024. That laser survey turned out to contain an entire ancient Maya city, hidden under forest cover for centuries. Aerial view of ancient ruins in Tulum. Photo credit: Dronepicr / Wikimedia Commons The survey used LiDAR, a mapping technique that fires laser pulses from an aircraft to measure distances to the ground. When you strip away the tree canopy from the data, you can see what’s underneath: in this case, pyramids, causeways, ball courts, and thousands of other structures in the southeastern Mexican state of Campeche. The organization that originally collected the data was monitoring the environment. They had no idea they’d flown over a lost city. Auld-Thomas and a fellow archaeologist named it Valeriana, after a nearby lagoon. Welcome to a lost Mayan metropolis The numbers are staggering. The city is thought to have housed an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 people at its peak, between roughly 750 and 850 AD. Its density may rank second only to Calakmul, one of the largest known Mayan cities. Researchers believe Valeriana may have served as a capital. Professor Marcello Canuto, a co-author on the research study and an anthropology professor at Tulane, said the discovery challenges a long-standing Western assumption that tropical regions were places “where civilization went to die.” The opposite appears to be true. These environments were densely settled, intensely developed, and home to sophisticated urban centers. In the area the team mapped, they identified more than 6,500 apparent structures. The find is part of a broader revolution in archaeology. LiDAR has been quietly rewriting what we know about ancient civilizations for over a decade. A 2013 study used the same technique to reveal massive urban networks around Angkor in Cambodia. In 2018, researchers used it to find more than 60,000 structures in the Guatemalan jungle. The technology lets archaeologists “digitally deforest” landscapes that would take lifetimes to survey on foot. A discovery hiding in plain sight What makes Valeriana striking is that nobody had to go anywhere to find it. The data had already been collected. It was just sitting in a file online, waiting for someone curious enough to click to page 16. Canuto noted that there are no actual photographs of Valeriana, only LiDAR maps, because no one has visited the site in person yet. As far as has been reported, the city remains swallowed by forest, traced only in laser points on a researcher’s screen, though researchers say they plan further fieldwork. “The point is that the landscape is definitely settled, that is, settled in the past, and not, as it appears to the naked eye, uninhabited or ‘wild,'” said Professor Elizabeth Graham of University College London . There’s likely more out there Canuto said in 2024 that he hopes for more funding and more drone-based mapping in the coming years. “It would be wonderful over the next 10, 20 years,” he said. “We should have double the amount of ground covered in LiDAR.” This means there are almost certainly more Valerianas out there hidden in plain sight, waiting for the next bored grad student to scroll far enough. This article originally appeared in May. It has been updated. The post Archaeology student found a lost Maya city on page 16 of a Google search appeared first on Upworthy .

Έρευνες δείχνουν ότι τα άτομα που περπατούν γρήγορα τε…
items.descriptionOriginal: There are two camps when it comes to walking speed: fast walkers and slow walkers . In a crowd of commuters, it’s easy to differentiate who is who. While fast walkers and slow walkers may irritate each other while trying to get from Point A to Point B, their differences go a lot deeper psychologically. Research suggests that people who walk fast tend to share certain personality traits, though the evidence is stronger for some than others. For example, fast walkers may be more conscientious. “Conscientiousness is the trait associated with organization, discipline, and reliability,” Christal Castagnozzi, Psychologist and Clinical Director at Thrive Psychology Health Team , tells Upworthy . “People high in this trait tend to manage their time well and move with intention. Research shows that fast walkers typically demonstrate goal-directed behavior which is a trademark of this trait. This often reflects their ability to be productive, stay on track, and efficient.” Personality traits of fast walkers These are six more personality traits that researchers and psychologists have linked to fast walking. They’re extraverted Fast walkers may also be more adventurous, though the research on this one is mixed. “Extraversion is the trait associated with being outgoing, energetic , and stimulated by social interaction,” says Castagnozzi. “These folks generally have higher activity levels and thrive in environments that keep them both physically and mentally engaged. Studies show that extraverts tend to move more and have energetic body language. A faster walking pace aligns with this as it reflects the elevated drive.” The ones that might surprise you most They’re low in neuroticism “Neuroticism refers to our worry, reactivity, and sensitivity to stress, so having low neuroticism would be the opposite: calm, resilient and steady,” Castagnozzi explains. “Large studies show that emotionally stable people walk faster, it is believed by researchers that this happens because they spend less energy on ruminating and dwelling and move with more confidence and ease.” New Yorkers have places to be. They walk miles every day in murky weather, moving quick to get from point A to point B. Californians (for example) aren’t like that. People take slower walks by the beach for fun or they run/hike. There is no in between. For destinations, we just… https://t.co/pNuOpe4gqr pic.twitter.com/5qntnnNlvh — micah (@micahfattahi) June 13, 2026 They’re open to new experiences Fast walkers may also be more adventurous. “Openness to experience is a trait associated with imagination, novelty, and curiosity,” adds Castagnozzi. “Although it doesn’t directly relate to walking speed, the novelty and excitement that is characteristic of this trait may lead to faster walking pace at times.” They’re agreeable The link between agreeableness and walking speed is less clear, but one psychologist says it may play a role. “Agreeableness is a trait associated with warmth, compassion, and cooperation,” Castagnozzi shares. “Individuals high in agreeableness may adjust their walking speed to match their walking partner so they may demonstrate a faster walking pace at times.” The personality traits of fast walkers. Photo credit: Canva And the ones that make total sense They’re assertive Fast walkers may also be bolder than slow walkers, according to one psychologist. “Assertiveness is a personality trait that is linked to confidence and taking initiative,” Castagnozzi says. “People that demonstrate this trait often tend to move with purpose and a clear sense of direction. Research supports that assertive individuals often display a faster walking pace.” They’re ambitious Fast walkers may also be go-getters, according to one psychologist. “Ambitiousness is a personality trait that is associated with an internal drive to grow and attain meaningful goals,” Castagnozzi explains. “Individuals may often carry a natural sense of urgency and a faster walking pace. These individuals have a tendency to value being efficient, having movement, and focusing on their intended targeted behavior.” Your pace says more than you think None of this means slow walkers are less driven or fast walkers are somehow better. Personality doesn’t work in absolutes, and neither does something as simple as how quickly you get from Point A to Point B. But it is a fun reminder that our bodies are constantly broadcasting little clues about who we are, long before we ever say a word. So the next time you catch yourself weaving through a crowd of slower walkers, or getting nudged to hurry up by someone speeding past you, know that it’s not really about the walk at all. It’s just one more small, honest signal of how you move through the rest of your life too. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Psychologist explains 7 personality traits of people who walk fast appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Going digital is often assumed to be a modern, efficient strategy that will save energy and resources: picture smart cities and industries humming along, with everything needed to run them stored cleanly in the cloud. The reality is just the opposite, according to a new study. Across 20 of the world’s largest economies, the growth of information technology has increased environmental burdens—largely because of the energy required to build and run digital infrastructure . In the new study, researchers gathered World Bank data on the G20 economies from 1990 through 2023. This group of large economies accounts for 80% of global GDP and 70% of carbon emissions. The researchers looked at three indicators of digitalization: internet usage, landline telephone subscriptions, and cellular subscriptions. They used a variety of statistical techniques to probe the direct and indirect associations between these indicators and carbon emissions. Past studies have established that information and communications technologies have yielded huge social and economic benefits for nations around the world, but the environmental consequences of these technologies have been less clear. Here's the carbon footprint of that. Strikingly, this pattern was almost entirely due to direct effects—that is, the energy needed to build and power digital infrastructure. “Data centers, device connectivity, and communication networks consume significant amounts of energy, which is largely sourced from carbon-intensive electricity,” the researchers write. The results suggest that the environmental benefits of digitalization depend on green electricity to power it—and at a global scale, that shift largely hasn’t happened yet. Clean energy is well known to be a key factor in determining the environmental benefits of electric cars . That relationship might not be as obvious in the case of digital technologies—it’s easy to overlook the energy required to make bits and bytes go bopping around the planet—but it’s no less crucial, the new work shows. The researchers expected that the early stages of digitalization, such as land line phone use, would be associated with increasing environmental burden but later stages, represented by internet and cellular adoption, with reduced carbon emissions—a pattern known as an environmental Kuznets curve. “In fact, economic and digital expansion continue to increase emissions rather than reduce them in the G20, revealing that these economies prioritize higher production and income over the cleaner environmental trajectory they often claim to pursue,” the researchers write. The upshot is that a push for digitalization needs to be accompanied by an effort to decarbonize the electricity that powers digital technologies, the researchers argue. Going forward, they say, governments should evaluate digitalization efforts not just in terms of technology access but also in terms of their climate impacts.
