items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News New Wild Cat Species Discovered in Bolivia Marks First Feline Find in Over a Century Reading Time: 3 minutes A new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia began its scientific journey when a rescuer mistook it for a lost kitten and fed it noodles, rice, and eggs, only to realize the tiny spotted animal was wild. The Leopardus tilcayo , now known as the tilcayo tiger cat, represents the first new living feline species formally described anywhere in the world in more than 100 years. This new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia inhabits the Yungas, the lush cloud forest ecotone where the Andes Mountains descend into the humid Amazon basin near La Paz. The discovery began unceremoniously. A resident living near the forest found the small, spotted animal and assumed it was a lost domestic kitten in need of help. He fed the creature noodles, rice, and eggs, but it failed to thrive on human food and soon began showing distinctly wild behaviors, prompting its transfer to the Senda Verde wildlife refuge once it became clear this was no ordinary house cat. What happened next transformed a rescue story into a scientific milestone. Researchers initially believed the animal belonged to Leopardus tigrinus, one of several already-recognized tiger cat species found across South America. Genetic analysis told a different story entirely. The new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia proved genetically distinct enough from its relatives to warrant classification as an entirely separate species, resolving what scientists call the tiger cat complex, a long-standing taxonomic puzzle now understood to comprise not one or two species, but five distinct ones. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who co-authored the study published in Current Biology and leads the Bolivian Felid Research and Conservation Program, emphasized how rare a discovery of this scale is. Finding any new, relatively large mammal remains uncommon in modern science, since most newly identified animal species are small invertebrates or microorganisms rather than mammals occupying visible ecological niches. Her National Geographic-funded conservation work underscored how much remains unknown about wild cat populations even today. Physically, the tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than an average house cat, measuring roughly 18 inches from head to body and weighing between three and five pounds. Its light brown coat is patterned with dark rosettes, making it look like a leopard shrunk down to kitten size. The species possesses shorter fur than the clouded tiger cat, while its tail is longer and fuller than that of the northern tiger cat yet less bushy than its clouded relative’s, distinguishing features researchers used alongside genetic evidence to confirm its status as a separate species. Researchers discovered this new wild cat species in Bolivia through a genomic analysis of 38 Leopardus specimens, combining museum skulls and modern samples to build a phylogenetic tree that revealed Leopardus tilcayo as genetically distinct, along with a newly recognized subspecies and the elevation of two other lineages to full species status. Photo courtesy of Current Biology . Despite global scientific excitement over this new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia, local communities throughout the Bolivian Yungas have known about the animal for generations, calling it tilcayo long before researchers formally documented it. This disconnect between indigenous ecological knowledge and formal scientific classification echoes a pattern seen repeatedly across biodiversity research worldwide, where species considered newly discovered by international science have often been recognized and named by local communities for far longer. The implications extend well beyond taxonomic bookkeeping. Scientists currently know very little about the tilcayo tiger cat’s population size, behavior, diet, or broader ecological role within the Yungas ecosystem. Confirming it as a distinct species carries meaningful conservation consequences, since protections and population assessments applied broadly to tiger cats as a group may not adequately address the specific needs or vulnerabilities facing this particular Bolivian lineage. Conservation organizations reacted to the discovery with a mix of celebration and renewed urgency. Stephanie Allard, Chief Mission Officer of the Dallas Zoo, described the finding as an exciting reminder of how much remains unknown about the natural world, a sentiment echoed throughout the global conservation community following the announcement. The new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia also highlights the Bolivian Yungas as a biodiversity hotspot that deserves far greater scientific attention and protection. This transitional forest zone, squeezed between high Andean peaks and lowland Amazonian rainforest, harbors ecological communities adapted to its unique elevation gradient and climate, conditions that likely shaped the genetic isolation allowing Leopardus tilcayo to diverge from its relatives in the first place. As researchers continue studying this newly confirmed species , fundamental questions remain unanswered: how many tilcayo tiger cats persist in the wild, what threats they face from habitat loss or human encroachment, and whether formal conservation status should follow their scientific recognition. For now, the discovery proves that even in an era of satellite mapping and genomic sequencing, Earth’s forests still conceal mammals entirely unknown to formal science, waiting only for the right combination of curiosity, rescue, and careful genetic analysis to bring them into view. The post New Wild Cat Species Discovered in Bolivia Marks First Feline Find in Over a Century appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: At Botton Village in North Yorkshire's moors, a philosophy researcher visits an old friend and finds something he didn't expect: a man transformed. Max, who had struggled to find his footing in conventional care arrangements, moves through the Esk Valley Camphill Community with what his friend describes as "a settled ease I hadn't seen in him before." His explanation is simple and quietly devastating: "It's been the best two years of my life. Much better than anything before." What the researcher gradually comes to understand - through months of shared meals, garden work, and community forums - is that Max hadn't just found better support. He had found a place where his presence mattered, where contribution and belonging were woven into the daily fabric of life rather than delivered on a schedule. The article raises a question that conventional social care policy rarely pauses long enough to ask: if what people most need is genuine community, what does it mean that we have built a system structurally designed to provide everything but that?

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Okanagan Nation Alliance Restores Salmon Access to Okanagan Lake Reading Time: 3 minutes The Okanagan Nation Alliance is restoring salmon access to Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly 100 years through a newly completed dam fish passage. The Okanagan Nation Alliance has reconnected sockeye salmon to Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly a century. A new fish passage now lets fish bypass a dam that has blocked the route since 1953. The milestone caps decades of restoration work led by Syilx Okanagan communities in British Columbia. Dams and channel work built through the last century cut salmon off from more than 350 square kilometers of lake habitat. The Okanagan Lake Dam at Penticton became one of the last major barriers standing in the salmon’s path. Until now, fish had no permanent route to swim safely around it. The Okanagan Nation Alliance runs one of Canada’s most extensive Indigenous-led fisheries programs. It comprises eight member communities and manages hatcheries, habitat restoration, and dam modifications across the Okanagan Basin. Its fisheries team has spent more than two decades working to bring salmon back. For Syilx Okanagan communities, the reconnection means more than fish counts. Elders describe a longstanding relationship between their people and salmon, one rooted in responsibility rather than simple resource use. Opening ceremonies for the passage included songs and drumming, along with tributes to community leaders who pushed for its construction over many years. Engineers designed the completed passage as a nature-like channel rather than a traditional metal fish ladder. Grating along the top lets sunlight reach the water and allows visitors to watch fish pass underneath. The Okanagan Nation Alliance’s completed fish passage is designed as a natural-looking channel rather than a traditional metal fish ladder, with grating along the top that lets sunlight reach the water and lets visitors watch fish pass underneath. Photo courtesy of Okanagan Nation Alliance . The route gives steelhead, rainbow trout, sockeye, chinook, and kokanee access to the lake and 13 tributary streams. An adjustable barrier built into the design filters out invasive species trying to follow the same path. That balance lets native fish through while keeping unwanted species out. Salmon runs in the Okanagan once numbered in the hundreds of thousands before dam construction and river channelization fragmented their habitat. The Okanagan Lake Dam, built in 1953, included an earlier fishway that never worked well. Water levels made it unusable for salmon during much of the year. The passage builds on a broader restoration effort the Okanagan Nation Alliance has carried out since the 1990s. That work includes a 12-year sockeye reintroduction program in nearby Skaha Lake and roughly 50 habitat projects across the basin. Modifications to two other dams further downstream have also opened additional spawning grounds. A conservation hatchery run by the Alliance raises sockeye fry each spring for release into historical spawning areas. Students take part in some releases through a program that introduces them to salmon biology and Syilx culture. In 2026 alone, organizers released 330,000 sockeye fry across the territory. Recovering salmon runs have also revived a small commercial and community fishery on Osoyoos Lake. In recent years, the Okanagan Nation Alliance’s fishing crew has landed record numbers of returning sockeye there, with thousands of fish distributed to member communities for ceremonies, trade, and food. A stronger run into Okanagan Lake could extend that momentum further north. Okanagan sockeye form part of a larger population that migrates through the Columbia River Basin shared by Canada and the United States. According to the International Joint Commission, Okanagan-origin fish account for the largest share of sockeye returning to that binational system most years. That transboundary status makes the newly reopened habitat significant well beyond British Columbia. International reviewers have noted the project’s design. The passage was nominated for the International Fish Passage Project of Distinction and presented at a fish passage conference in California in 2026. Recognition like this signals growing interest in Indigenous-led approaches to river restoration. Returns to the reopened habitat are expected to stay modest at first, since warm river conditions have limited recent salmon numbers. Even so, the passage will remain open for every future migration season. For a Nation that has worked for generations to see salmon return, a permanent route into Okanagan Lake marks a turning point rather than an ending. items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τη Megan Kuykendoll, καθηγήτρια οικογενειακής επιστήμης και κοινωνικής εργασίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Μαϊάμι, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Όταν γεννήθηκε το δεύτερο παιδί μας, ο σύζυγός μου είχε s…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Megan Kuykendoll , an instructor of family science and social work at Miami University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work. I’m a certified family life educator , and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work. So I was aware of the benefits his leave could have for our family — in theory. Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community. During his leave time, my spouse took our oldest child to playdates and birthday parties. He quickly became connected with our small-town network of families with kids close in age. I witnessed my spouse becoming more comfortable being the “main” parent in public, going to kid-centered community events, and connecting with other parents. Our family is still seeing the benefits of those few weeks 10 years later. Leave for supporting parents after the birth of a child isn’t standardized or required by law in most places in the U.S. Even countries with generous paid time off for the birthing parent don’t always offer similarly generous time for the non-birthing parent. This diversity in leave policies can make it hard to assess the impact of leave for the non-birthing parent. But existing research suggests that extended leave for birthing parents and moderate leave for non-birthing partners positively impact infant well-being and reduce postpartum mental health challenges. Maternal and Newborn Health Leave for both parents with the birth of a child can significantly benefit parental mental health overall and maternal mental health specifically . Paternity leave assists in the mother’s recovery and contributes to less of an increase in stress and depression than for mothers whose partners didn’t take leave. One Swedish study showed that flexibility within paternal leave policies, such as allowing new dads to take intermittent time off after the birth of a child, helped reduce the incidence of maternal postpartum health complications . Children also benefit from paternity leave. When a father takes significant leave — meaning at least two weeks — children report experiencing more father-child closeness and better communication in the relationship up to nine years later. And overall child health tends to improve when fathers take paternity leave. When paid leave policies are available for both mothers and fathers , breastfeeding is more likely to last longer. Longer breastfeeding is strongly linked to overall infant health and decreased infant mortality . SolStock—E+/Getty Images Paternity leave is an opportunity for fathers to become comfortable in their parenting role and connect with other parents. Family Balance Allowing both parents to have sufficient time off to bond and adjust to their new roles can also have longer-term benefits within the family unit and contribute toward more equity in child rearing. Even in 2026, mothers are often considered the “default” parent, with fathers taking a more secondary role . While fathers are more involved now than in previous generations, mothers are still more likely to be the first call from school. And even with an involved father, mothers continue to carry the invisible mental load of the family , an unseen burden of data, obligations, and preemptive planning tasks. This overreliance on mothers comes with a price: Mothers report being more stressed and tired than fathers do. As I experienced in my own family, when fathers have ample time off, it sets up the dynamic to be more balanced between parents. This helps reduce the strain on recovering mothers and redistributes some of the care work that goes into raising children. Home Economics What’s more, paid leave policies have been shown to help families’ financial health . Pay rates during leave can vary widely depending on your company, organization, or country. Without full or close to full pay, many families cannot afford to take leave. In the U.S., for example, the Family and Medical Leave Act allows time off, but not in all circumstances , nor is that time required to be paid. Many families cannot afford to take the full allowable time off, using up sick or vacation time if available. Many parents in the U.S. end up going back to work sooner than seems healthy . New parents in the U.S. often find themselves in an economic bind — they can’t afford to take leave, nor can they afford to rely on a single income to have a parent stay home. But many also can’t afford the childcare rates for newborns, which tend to be particularly high. National averages for infant care at childcare centers are nearly $200 more per month than toddler care. While rates vary significantly depending on where you live and what type of care you choose, infant care remains the most expensive . Despite the lack of a paid U.S. federal leave policy for parents, both domestic and multinational companies have noticed that their workers care about parental leave policies. Some have begun to offer leave for supporting parents in order to recruit and retain workers . Outside the US U.S. leave policies consistently rank at or near the bottom when compared with other similarly developed countries, like the 38 members of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, or OECD. Some countries follow a “use-it-or-lose-it” model of parental leave, where fathers in particular are encouraged to take a more substantial role in childcare. Sweden and Norway, for example, earmark 90 days of leave for each parent, and it cannot be transferred to or split with the other parent. This encourages both parents to take time off. There are many options across countries with parental leave policies. Flexibility and defined expectations seem to be key contributors to getting the most out of the parental leave that is offered. Cultural Adoption When non-birthing parents are men, another barrier to taking leave is the perceived social acceptability within their communities. Even when paid paternity leave is available, many men struggle to take it because of how traditional gender roles and expectations of masculinity frame childcare as women’s work . To offset these kinds of social pressures, countries like Japan and Austria offer incentives such as bonus leave time for families when fathers actually take their available leave. Germany offers a similar bonus, and it has found improved couple relationship satisfaction when fathers take more of their leave time. Beyond improvements in maternal and infant health, both parents taking leave can create a more equitable workplace environment . Disparities and discrimination that come when only women take leave after birth can lessen when fathers and other supporting parents also take leave. Childbearing women are then less likely to be penalized, formally or informally, for taking parental leave. Paid parental leave policies that provide leave for all parents, regardless of gender, also can help reduce structural inequality in the workplace across race and class. In the U.S., Hispanic and Black workers often have less access to paid leave policies and may experience increased pressure to return to work earlier than their white counterparts. As more states, countries, and corporations adopt more flexible and inclusive leave policies, researchers will continue to learn how parental leave benefits both parents and children. What they’ve found so far leads me to believe that, just like we’ve seen with prenatal care and early education programs , parental leave will prove to be an early investment in healthy children and families that pays dividends in the long term. Εκπαιδευτής σκύλων Sassafras Patte…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s something about crisp fall air that makes you want to get outside, and if you have a dog, you’ve probably noticed they feel it too: the extra pull on the leash when the leaves start to turn, the way they pause longer than usual to investigate every scent the new season brings. Dog trainer Sassafras Patterdale says fall is one of the best times of year to take your dog somewhere new, partly because the cooler temperatures make longer outings more comfortable, and partly because places like farmers’ markets, pumpkin patches , and hiking trails offer something a backyard walk can’t: a real chance for your dog to build confidence around new people, places, and experiences, while you practice skills like loose-leash walking around genuine distractions. A little planning goes a long way Before heading out anywhere new, Patterdale recommends thinking through your dog’s comfort level with crowds. Younger puppies and newly adopted dogs who are still building confidence tend to do better at quieter times, like weekday visits or early weekend mornings, while dogs who are comfortable around people and other animals may be ready for busier gatherings. Neither is wrong; it just depends on where your dog is right now. Pack a few essentials: water and a portable bowl, treats for rewarding good behavior, and poop bags. A properly fitted harness or collar and a standard six-foot leash are good to have in any busy area, and depending on the weather and your dog’s coat, a sweater or jacket may be a smart call for smaller or short-haired dogs. Farmers market A farmers market is one of the more dog-friendly fall outings. The mix of people, other animals, food smells, and steady foot traffic gives your dog plenty of opportunities to practice calm, attentive behavior on leash, and plenty of reasons to earn a treat. Patterdale recommends offering praise and treats whenever your dog walks calmly at your side or glances back to check in with you. Those little check-ins are what you want to encourage. Keep your dog close and prevent them from sniffing or pawing at food displays, and be mindful of shoppers who may not be comfortable around dogs. Most farmers markets welcome well-behaved, leashed dogs, but policies vary by location, so confirm before you go. Pumpkin patch A pumpkin patch visit makes for good seasonal photos, and dogs tend to enjoy the outing for their own reasons entirely. The open space, interesting smells, and steady stream of new things to look at give them a lot to engage with, and it’s a naturally good setting to practice cues like “stay” somewhere unfamiliar and exciting. Patterdale recommends checking the farm’s pet policy before arriving, since some farms restrict dogs in certain areas, particularly active harvest fields, for food safety reasons. Farms that host seasonal activities often welcome leashed dogs in the public areas, so a quick call or website check usually settles it. Corn maze If the farm also runs a corn maze, it can be a fun extension of the visit. The winding paths give dogs a chance to sniff and explore at their own pace, which Patterdale says is some of the best mental stimulation you can offer on a walk. One thing to watch for: avoid letting your dog round corners ahead of you, since that can startle other visitors, particularly children, or lead to an unexpected run-in with another dog. Haunted corn mazes are generally better skipped, since the loud noises and sudden surprises tend to be overwhelming for most dogs, even confident ones. As always, confirm the pet policy before you go. Hiking trail For a quieter option that lets you and your dog set your own pace, a fall hike is hard to beat. Many state and local parks welcome leashed dogs, and autumn trails give dogs a lot to work with: the crunch of leaves underfoot, the smell of damp earth, the cool air that seems to make dogs want to cover more ground than usual. Patterdale recommends allowing extra time so your dog can stop to sniff and investigate along the way. Dogs experience a huge portion of the world through their noses, and giving them space to follow a scent or linger over a fallen log makes the whole outing more satisfying for both of you. Check park regulations before heading out, since rules about dogs on trails vary by location and trail type. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Water has always been part of how many American cities move people, but for most of the country’s history it has been an afterthought compared to roads and rails. A new generation of electric ferries is beginning to change that, and some of them work in a way that is surprising: they handle the problem of water by getting out of it. The physics problem that held electric boats back Electrifying boats has always been harder than electrifying cars, and the reason comes down to drag. Water resists a moving vessel far more than air resists a moving vehicle, which means boats require substantially more energy per mile. That high energy demand, combined with the weight of batteries, has made it difficult to design an electric vessel that can carry enough passengers far enough to be useful as everyday transit. Hydrofoils get around this in a way that seems almost too obvious once you hear it. These vessels use underwater wings to lift the hull clear of the water as they accelerate, and once the hull is airborne, drag drops sharply. Vessev , a company that builds fully electric hydrofoil boats, says its design cuts drag by about 66 percent, which lets the boats carry smaller, lighter battery packs without sacrificing range. “We substantially reduce the drag that you feel, and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” said Eric Laakmann , Vessev’s chief executive and co-founder. What the ride is like The transition happens fast. As a Vessev boat accelerates through New York Harbor, the hydrofoils push the hull about a foot and a half above the surface, and the sensation of a boat working against waves gives way almost immediately to something smoother and quieter, closer to gliding than crossing water. “We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said during a recent demonstration, drawing curious looks from passengers on a nearby sightseeing ferry. His company is still a novelty to most people on the water, and he knows it. From demonstration to daily commute Vessev operates passenger services in New Zealand, with Australia next and its first US route planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann’s ambition runs past tourism: he wants electric vessels to be as unremarkable as buses, something commuters use because it’s there. “More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said. That idea has already taken root in parts of Europe. Stockholm commuters are riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela, which says its design uses as much as 80 percent less energy than conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of the same boats for coastal service. The US is later to this shift, but several cities are starting to move. San Francisco prepares for a half-billion-dollar overhaul San Francisco carries about 3.5 million ferry passengers a year across a region shaped by its bay, and every one of the 18 vessels in the current fleet runs on diesel. Four battery-powered ferries are set to join the fleet over the next two years as part of an electric overhaul worth roughly half a billion dollars, including new charging infrastructure at its docks. Converting a ferry network is more complicated than swapping out a car fleet. Ferries run on fixed schedules and cannot stop mid-route to recharge, so operators have to design the entire system around the relationship between battery range, trip time, and how much power the shoreside chargers can deliver in the minutes a vessel sits at the terminal. Seamus Murphy, who runs the agency, put it plainly: “We have a lot of waterfront.” San Francisco’s new vessels won’t use hydrofoil technology , but the agency says they’ll make it the first ferry operator in the country to run high-speed, all-electric service. The economics of a fleet switch For a long time, the financial math and the environmental math didn’t add up at the same time. Battery-powered ferries cost more upfront, but electric motors tend to be more efficient than diesel engines, and the savings on fuel and maintenance accumulate. Rising diesel costs have shifted the balance, as has continued progress in battery technology. “You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time, and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” Murphy said. How well that holds up depends on the route: long distances, tight turnaround windows, and limited charging opportunities can all make the switch impractical. Not every waterway is suited to a fully electric vessel. For shorter commuter routes in cities with the right geography, though, the numbers are starting to work. For San Francisco’s expansion, both the boats and their batteries are being manufactured in the US. Murphy sees this as a window that won’t stay open indefinitely. “These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” he said. “We don’t want to be left behind.” Water as working transit Transportation is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the US, and watercraft burning diesel contribute their share, particularly around busy ports and waterfront neighborhoods. Electric ferries could cut both emissions and the localized air pollution that diesel docks generate, while also opening up routes that weren’t previously viable and connecting communities by water without the cost of new roads or rail. It won’t happen all at once. Some cities will move fast; others will take years to follow. But the direction looks clear. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said, standing on a boat that had just crossed a harbor without burning a drop of fuel. Αλλά βγάζουν τα χρήματά τους με μεγάλες πιθανότητες και παιχνίδια που φαίνονται κερδισμένα αλλά συνήθως δεν είναι. Ένας κλασικός γρίφος απλοποιεί την εξίσωση an…
items.descriptionOriginal: Pretty much everyone would be overjoyed at the thought of being given some free money. But how much of that free money would you be willing to risk to double it ? It sounds like a question for the Las Vegas casinos. But they make their money with long odds, and games that seem winnable but usually aren’t. A classic riddle simplifies the equation and, in doing so, brings up a fascinating debate between human psychology and raw math. The two envelope problem explained Content creator Joey Rogoff recently shared something of a riddle on his Facebook page . “You’re given two envelopes. One contains exactly twice as much money as the other. You choose one and open it to find $100. You’re now offered the chance to switch envelopes. Would you switch?” It’s a variation on a classic prompt called the “two envelope problem.” In essence, the question says that you could walk away with $100, or you could choose the other envelope which has an equal shot at being either $50 or $200. What would you do? Joey Rogoff started quite a stir when he shared the two envelope problem. Joey Rogoff/ Facebook The mathematically correct answer is… The math behind the riddle is simple… at first. We assume the other envelope has equal odds of containing either $50 or $200. That puts the EV, Expected Value, of opening the other envelope at $125—it’s the average of the two possible outcomes. If you did the exercise a billion times, you’d come out ahead by switching. Simple. Where things start to get a little confounding is if you leave both envelopes closed. You select one, your chosen envelope, but don’t open it quite yet. If you are given the choice of switching in that split second before you find out what’s inside, the math says the same thing: The other envelope yields a 1.25 EV. So you switch, and choose the other one. But before you open that one, the math again suggests that you should switch back . See the problem? It creates an infinite loop. A paradox . Lucky for us, mathematicians have been hard at work on the two envelope problem for years. The problem with the logic above is that, in the real world, not all outcomes are equally likely. If the scenario were real, there would have to be a top limit, or a budget. There could be no infinity dollars inside one of the choices. So the bigger the number you’d find in your original envelope, the less likely you would be to want to switch; both because the odds that the other envelope contained double your already large amount get smaller, and because the potential loss would hurt far more. However, for Rogoff’s hypothetical version, where the first envelope contains $100, it feels like you should switch, even if the math behind it is a little murky. Psychology shows why the problem has people divided Even if you feel like switching is the right choice, your actions might get overridden by another feeling all together. A commenter on Rogoff’s post made a salient point when he wrote, “I fully understand the math logic in most of the other comments about switching, but I would stand pat. Whenever I have an either/or choice, I always make the wrong choice. Every time. I know no matter what I do will be wrong, so I would rather be wrong with $100 than with $50.” And this commenter wasn’t the only one. For every person who understood that the probability of walking away with more money was better with a switch, there was another person too afraid of losing the $50 to pull the trigger. “I’m taking the $100 and walking away. Most of y’all need to stay away from casinos.” “You can’t lose money you don’t win. Only on money you possess. That means keeping the $100 isn’t you losing $100 if you didn’t get the $200 by switching. You DO lose money if you switch and the other envelope only has $50” There’s clearly something larger at play in this problem than just mathematics. What the pure numbers don’t account for is something psychologists call loss aversion . It’s a cognitive bias that says the pain of losing something is worse than the joy of an equivalent gain. In this context, many people feel that losing out on $50 would not be worth the potential thrill of winning an extra $100. It’s a fascinating concept. Many experts argue that loss aversion holds us back and impairs our ability to make the best decisions in many areas of life: career, money, dating, friendships. But sometimes that deep fear of losing out protects us. For example, what if the two envelope problem wasn’t a hypothetical game, but a real scenario, and you needed the money to pay rent? Risking the switch would be difficult for most people in that scenario, even though the math would stay the same. The two envelope problem is such a classic because you can argue about it forever and never be wrong. It’s a fantastic litmus test for our risk tolerance, and even if the math gets a little shaky in hypothetical-land, your response to the riddle can tell you a lot about how you make decisions. The post The classic ‘two envelope problem’ riddle pits math against psychology appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Η μητέρα του Owen Thiele είχε ήδη πάρει την απόφασή της. Ήταν στο Τέξας και ήθελε ο γιος της να έχει μια οικογένεια κοντά, άτομα με τα οποία θα μπορούσε να έχει επαφή. Ένα ζευγάρι στο Λος Άντζελες δεν ταίριαζε. «Η μητέρα μου που γεννήθηκα ήθελε πραγματικά κάποιον ντόπιο, κάποιον στο Τέξας, κάποιον με τον οποίο θα μπορούσε ίσως να έχει σχέση», Thiele, η « Ενήλικες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Owen Thiele’s birth mother had already made her decision . She was in Texas, and she wanted her son placed with a family nearby, people she might be able to stay in touch with . A couple in Los Angeles didn’t fit. “My birth mom really wanted someone local, someone in Texas, someone who she could maybe have a relationship with,” Thiele, the “ Adults ” actor, said in September on Tish Cyrus’s podcast, “ Sorry We’re Cyrus .” Rather than leave it to the agency, she called the couple herself. “Eventually my birth mom called my mom, I think, as a courtesy to be like, ‘I’m kind of going in a different direction here,’” Thiele said. Nobody picked up so it went to the answering machine. The greeting was Thiele’s dad tickling his mom while she tried, and failed, to get through it without laughing. That’s all it took change everything. “My birth mom was like, ‘I need my son to be filled with laughter and joy, and I want him to be around… support and love,’” Thiele said. Her message to the couple was simple: “Come pick up your kid.” View this post on Instagram Thiele, now 30, also stars in Prime Video’s “ Overcompensating .” He and Cyrus had met at Raven-Symoné’s birthday party, where they figured out within minutes that they’d both been adopted at birth. He was born in Houston in 1996 and raised in Beverly Hills by music producer Bob Thiele Jr. and Amy Kanter. Growing up as a Black kid in a white Jewish family is now the basis of his upcoming comedy series, “ Off Color ,” which he’ll star in, write and co-executive produce. The post A birth mother called to reject an adoption. Their answering machine greeting changed her mind. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Μια αναφορά ειδήσεων του Ουισκόνσιν του 1991 δεν είχε μεγάλες ελπίδες για τη νεολαία Gen X. Τους αποδείξαμε ότι έκαναν λάθος.
items.titleOriginal: A 1991 Wisconsin news report didn’t have high hopes for Gen X youth. We proved them wrong.
items.description: Μερικές φορές, χρειάζεται εκ των υστέρων σκέψη για να καταλάβουμε την ουσία μιας γενιάς. Για παράδειγμα, οι Boomers δεν γνώριζαν ενώ ενηλικιώνονταν ότι το γένος τους θα οδηγούσε σε εκρηκτική αύξηση του πληθυσμού. Συχνά χρειάζονται χρόνια για να δούμε και να αναλύσουμε τις τάσεις. Έτσι, όταν το WMTV Channel 15, ένας ειδησεογραφικός σταθμός στο Ουισκόνσιν, δημοσίευσε μια ειδική αναφορά για το πώς ο Gen…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sometimes, it takes hindsight to figure out the essence of a generation. For example, the Boomers didn’t know while they were coming of age that their gen would lead to an explosive growth of the population. It often takes years to see and analyze the trends. So when WMTV Channel 15, a news station in Wisconsin, put out a special report of how Gen X was shaping up, it would be impossible to know if their predictions were correct. The year was 1991, when Gen X was entering college and early adulthood. (A few of the younger X-ers were just finishing up high school.) The exposé was focused on how, for the first time in American history, many of this 80s/90s generation were facing more hardship than their parents. View this post on Instagram ‘What TV news thought of Gen X’ A chyron reading, “What TV News thought of Gen X back in 1991” floats at the top of the clip , posted by 90s Rock Vault . Two news reporters sit behind a desk, the woman wearing an 80s-styled white blazer, complete with linebacker-sized shoulder pads. She shares, “This is the first generation facing adulthood believing that life for them may not be as good as it was for their parents. It’s creating a generation whose only reality is simply a future in doubt.” The clip cuts to a person wearing headphones as they lie on a backpack. Nirvana’s “Smells Like Teen Spirit” screams in the background, as the camera cuts to young people strewn across college campuses. “There is a sense of insecurity, which is probably realistic.” Another voice is heard saying, “And you worry about, you know, just getting a job.” The 13th Gen We hear the reporter add, “It adds up to a lot of anxiety that shows up in their music, their clothes and their attitude. Often misinterpreted and misunderstood, about the only thing they are certain of is that they are uncertain. They are Generation X, the 13th Gen.” They cut to an interview with Victor Ferrall, the then President of Beloit College. He explains, “If you start from Ben Franklin and count forward in American history, this is the 13th generation of Americans.” The reporter continues, “Growing up in the economic upheaval of the 70s and 80s, weaned on Sesame Street and MTV, most 20-somethings accept their unique situation. Their life will not be like their parents’.” We flash back to Ferrall, who further shares, “There’s a huge change in America. Just for the entire history of our country, people have always believed that life would be better for their children than it was for them.” Over photos of people walking down a busy street in the ’90s, the reporter adds, “…until Generation X. They watched inflation balloon their parents’ paychecks. And now they search for the real value in everything they do.” ‘Without all the hype’ She holds a microphone up to a young woman. “Realistic. ‘Real’ is the main thing that we’re looking at. Something that’s real with, yeah, without all the hype and the gimmicks and things like that. It’s our whole mentality.” Roseanne Cheeseman, of Directions Magazine, jokes, “That whole thing about waiting till you can get your big break into the burger industry. You know what I mean? And a lot of that is tongue in cheek. I think that a lot of the cynicism on the part of Generation X is not so much being 100 percent disillusioned with their chances in the world, but a lot of it is just making fun of the situation.” “Generation X,” the news reporter shares, “ponders whether the future holds happiness.” For that thought, they throw it over to Gerald Marwell, a Sociology Professor at University of Washington. “People in the ’60s,” he says, “had a pretty good idea…they thought that they were going to be like, in a sense, their parents. They were going to get married. They were going to have kids.” The divorce revolution When it came to Gen X, the concept of commitment was reimagined. Young adults dressed in red and black flannel shirts are shown as the reporter continues. “And while the flower children were protesting and fighting for social change, they started a revolution.” (“The divorce revolution,” Marwell states.) She relays, “Generation X grew up smack dab in the middle of it.” The report then interviews a young woman, wearing all black, her ear riddled with earrings. “A lot of people, I don’t think, expect to be happy in relationships. Cuz that’s what they saw.” Another woman adds, “I think a lot of people are leery of that and would like to have a longer relationship before they get into the commitment of marriage.” Marwell explains, “The kids today aren’t really sure what their lives are going to be like. They aren’t sure how many kids they’re gonna have. They’re not sure they’re gonna have any kids. They’re not sure of what’s going to happen to them.” Finally, Ferrall shares, “Parents had uncertain values to pass on to their kids. And economic uncertainty to pass on to them. And it left young people kind of rootless. Kind of unsure of themselves.” Gen X now Now, 35 years later, we have a true sense of how Gen X fits into the world. Despite the uncertainty, many are often quite successful. Kieran Smith writes, “After college, Gen X continued to succeed in the workplace, resulting in a generation financially outcompeting those around them. According to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the median income of American workers reaches its peak between the ages of 45 and 54, roughly the age of most Gen Xers.” Generation X, despite the cynical jokes and often dark music, are also deemed by some to be the happiest generation. In a recent piece I wrote for Upworthy, I quoted Alene Dawson’s 2011 article “Study Says Generation X is balanced and happy,” for CNN. She cites University of Michigan’s The Generation X Report , which claims Gen Xers (who at the time were between 30–45) are ‘active, balanced and happy.’” Don’t let the grunge rock fool you. While some of us might have been handed a plate of lemons, we squeezed as much out as possible to make lemonade. The post A 1991 Wisconsin news report didn’t have high hopes for Gen X youth. We proved them wrong. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το Open Campus. Περνώντας από το συμβουλευτικό γραφείο του New River μια μέρα, η Stephanie Addikis παρατήρησε ότι τα βιβλία ζωγραφικής και τα Lego που είχε βοηθήσει να αποθηκεύσουν σε ένα κοντινό κουτί ήταν… «πολύ αγαπημένα». Αυτό ακριβώς ήλπιζε ότι θα συμβεί. Το «απασχολημένο κουτί» με παιχνίδια είναι μέρος μιας νέας προσπάθειας στο New River για προμήθεια…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Open Campus . W alking by New River’s advising office one day, Stephanie Addikis noticed that the coloring books and Legos that she had helped stock in a nearby box were … “well-loved.” This was just what she was hoping would happen. The “busy box” stuffed with toys is part of a new effort at New River to support parenting students. When students are filling out the FAFSA or visiting with their adviser, they can bring their children and know they will have toys nearby to entertain them. “I don’t think we realized how many kids were coming on campus until we put these out, and now they’re really being utilized,” said Addikis, who is the adult career coach and community outreach specialist at New River. New River Community College is working to integrate more support for parenting students throughout campus. Courtesy of New River Community College A report released a couple weeks ago from The Institute for College Access & Success, or TICAS, showed that about a quarter of students attending rural-serving institutions are parents. But those colleges are also less likely to have childcare on campus than their non-rural counterparts. A lack of data on the number of parenting students is one of the biggest challenges for colleges trying to support them, according to one of the authors of that report, Erika Roberson. There’s a reason that Addikis was so excited to see used toys on campus: She does not know exactly how many parent students go to New River. While at least five states have now required public colleges to ask students if they have children, and Virginia just passed similar legislation this spring , the lack of standardized data collection makes serving these students even more difficult. And supporting them matters because student parents are more likely to be students of color, low-income and the first in their families to go to college. Those challenges combined make them less likely to graduate than their non-parenting peers. But, like rural places do, these colleges are getting creative in expanding support even with limited data and funding. To collect more thorough data, Roane State Community College in eastern Tennessee is partnering with Achieving the Dream . Others are collaborating with local churches, women shelters, groups like United Way and other nonprofits to connect student parents with resources. Our reporter at partner newsroom The Fort Worth Report, Dang Le, recently reported on new childcare centers that opened at Tarrant County College with the support of the college, county and a childcare nonprofit. “Not all these schools are receiving robust grants to do this work,” Roberson said. “Maybe there are existing partnerships that schools have that they might be able to tap into to more explicitly support their student parents, or maybe there are ways in which they can modify syllabi to include family-friendly policies that don’t have dollar signs on it.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Rather than one new program, it’s a cultural shift that student parents are looking for, according to another recent report focused on six public rural-serving colleges and universities in California . In other words, student parents want to feel seen — by their counselors, advisers, professors and other staff members or peers. While parents make up a large portion of students at rural-serving schools, it’s common for these students to still feel isolated . That’s why several colleges featured in the TICAS report are starting peer parenting groups and hosting events. New River, for example, has a dedicated family study room with child-sized furniture in their library (which also serves as a public library) and consistently hosts events or dinners for students and faculty with children. New River provides care packages for new and expecting parents, including diapers, wipes, a Walmart gift card and t-shirts. Courtesy of New River Community College Addikis said she felt this cultural shift even more prominently at New River when funding to parent-support programs decreased. New River was one of the first five colleges to receive the College Attainment for Parent Students grants from the Virginia Foundation for Community College Education. In those first couple of years, the college created cohorts of 20 student parents, and each parent was eligible for $2,000 stipends per semester, including summer semesters. Now, the foundation associated with the community college system gives each of the 23 schools some funding, so the grant amounts have decreased. New River adjusted by starting an application process, and they granted 17 students $500 each this year. Addikis said more than half of the students who applied said they rely on friends and family for childcare, so this stipend will likely help reimburse things like gas or food. But with fewer financial resources, Addikis started to look at what she could do to grow relationships with these student parents and remind them that they are not on their own. For example, she has a work-study student who is also a parent this semester, and that student is planning to start a student parent club on campus. The challenge, she said, still remains in increasing awareness about the resources on campus. One thing that she said helped was creating a section of their first-year orientation course specifically for adult learners and highlighting resources available for parents. “I see it now as a warm hug, and a lot of love and support and just a building of awareness,” she said, talking about how the parent support has changed with less funding. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Still, researchers like those at TICAS still advocate for increased data and funding for student parent support, especially on rural campuses. Two federal grant programs in particular focus on this area: Childcare Access Means Parents in Schools and Basic Needs for Postsecondary Students. “I don’t want policymakers to forget rural parenting students,” Roberson said. “And if policymakers are really interested in strengthening rural economies, I think it’s important that they also invest in rural parenting students.” The post Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Η αποκατάσταση της Χρυσής Στέπας του Καζακστάν έχει προκαλέσει μία από τις μεγαλύτερες ανακτήσεις άγριας ζωής που έχουν καταγραφεί. Οι αριθμοί των αντιλόπες Saiga έχουν ανέβει f…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe Reading Time: 3 minutes Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has helped saiga antelope rebound from about 20,000 to 4.6 million. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has produced one of the largest wildlife recoveries on record. Saiga antelope numbers have climbed from roughly 20,000 in the early 2000s to about 4.6 million in 2026. The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative has led this work since 2006. Altyn Dala means “golden steppe” in Kazakh. The initiative has helped protect 5 million hectares of grassland, an area larger than Denmark. It is also bringing back wild asses and wild horses that vanished from the region long ago. The saiga is a small antelope with a large, flexible nose that filters dust and warms cold air. Its herds migrate hundreds of miles across the steppe, a vast, dry grassland with few trees. By the early 2000s, those herds had nearly disappeared. After the Soviet Union collapsed, poaching surged across Central Asia. Hunters killed saigas for meat and for male horns, which sold for traditional medicine in Asia. Within about a decade, the population crashed by more than 95%. Five partners joined forces in 2006 to reverse that decline. Kazakhstan’s Committee for Forestry and Wildlife works with the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan. Fauna & Flora, the Frankfurt Zoological Society, and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds bring international support. Their first priority was stopping the killing. Ranger teams and aerial patrols now cover the saiga’s range. Sniffer dogs and customs training help catch horn smugglers at the border. Next, the partners needed to know where the herds went. Since 2009, researchers have fitted saigas with satellite tags to map their migrations. That data shows which areas need protection and when. New reserves followed the herds. The most recent, Bokey Orda-Ashiozek in western Kazakhstan, covers about 657,000 hectares. Wildlife corridors also link reserves through private land, under joint plans with landowners. The strategy faced its hardest test in 2015. During the spring calving season, more than 200,000 saigas died within weeks, over 60% of the global population. A 2018 study in Science Advances linked the deaths to a bacterium that turned deadly in hot, humid weather. Because poaching was under control, the surviving herds could rebuild. Aerial surveys each spring tracked the comeback. The 2024 count found about 2.8 million saigas, and the 2026 count reached roughly 4.6 million. That is about 230 times the low point. In December 2023, the IUCN Red List moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened. The Kazakh association’s director, Vera Voronova, called it one of the most successful land mammal recoveries ever recorded. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe means rebuilding the full community of grazing animals, not just one species. Kulan, a wild ass native to Central Asia, disappeared from the Torgai steppe more than 100 years ago. Scientists consider them a keystone species, since their grazing and movement help shape the grassland. Reintroductions began in 2017, and partners aim to establish about 100 kulan in the region. A recent group traveled 2,139 kilometers by road from Altyn-Emel National Park. After a year in an acclimatization pen, the animals went free in August 2025. Przewalski’s horses are following the same path. Considered the last truly wild horse species, they vanished from the wild by 1969 and survived only in zoos. In Kazakhstan, they had been gone for about 200 years. Przewalski’s horses returning to the wild are part of restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe after about 200 years. Photo by Wijs (Wise) on Pexels. The first seven horses arrived at the Altyn Dala reserve in 2024. More followed in 2025 from Prague Zoo and Hungary’s Hortobágy National Park. In May 2026, five of them left their pens and began roaming free. Officials plan to bring 40 to 45 horses by 2029, enough to sustain the herd. A stallion named Galvan wears a GPS collar so rangers can follow his movements. Local support makes these gains last. The initiative runs education programs in rural schools and has published children’s books about steppe wildlife in Kazakh. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe depends on the next generation valuing these animals. Recovery has also created new tensions. Farmers in several regions report that saigas damage crops and compete with livestock for pasture. Authorities are now studying how to manage herd sizes without undoing two decades of conservation. Roads, railways, and fences still break up migration routes. Wildfires and farm expansion put pressure on ground-nesting birds. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe will require balancing people and wildlife for years to come. Twenty years ago, the saiga seemed headed for extinction. Today, millions roam the plains, joined by wild asses and horses returning after a century or more. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe shows what patient, well-coordinated protection can achieve. The post Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Αντί να τα εγκαταλείψει όλα, δημοσίευσε μια ανώνυμη πρόσκληση στα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης και 11 γυναίκες από τις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες, τον Καναδά και την Ουαλία είπαν ναι - σε έναν ξένο, μια χώρα, μια…
items.descriptionOriginal: When Bridget Devaney's engagement ended after her fianc 's medical emergency, she was left holding plans for a trip to Northern Ireland and a wedding day that would never come. Rather than abandon it all, she posted an anonymous invitation on social media, and 11 women from the United States, Canada, and Wales said yes - to a stranger, a country, and an uncertain week. "When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," Bridget told BBC News NI. On the day originally reserved for her wedding, the women dressed up and stood together against Northern Ireland's coastline for photographs that captured something the original plans never could have. What the trip quietly reveals is how much people are willing to show up for one another -- and how belonging can find us even in the ruins of what we thought our lives would look like.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News American Red Wolf Pups Fostered into the Wild in North Carolina Reading Time: 3 minutes American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild bring fresh genes to a critically endangered species. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild mark a first in Saint Louis Zoo history. Three critically endangered, zoo-born pups now live with a wild Red Wolf family in North Carolina. Fewer than 40 American Red Wolves remain in the wild. They live only in northeastern North Carolina. That group would not even fill a single school bus. The wolves are critically endangered, which means they face a very high risk of extinction. Hunters nearly wiped them out in the 1800s and 1900s. They once roamed the southeastern United States and are native nowhere else. In the 1960s, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) teamed up with North American zoos. Together, they started a breeding and reintroduction program for the species. The three pups were born at the zoo’s Sears Lehmann, Jr. Wildlife Reserve. Staff collected them on April 20, when they were seven days old. They underwent a health exam before the trip. Zoo staff traveled with the pups to the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge in northeast North Carolina. They cared for the pups hour by hour along the way. FWS biologists then placed them in a wild den, a shelter where a mother raises her young. Biologists watched the den to see whether the wild mother returned. She did, and she accepted the newcomers into her litter. Several months later, the pups began exploring outside the den, and trail cameras showed all three alive and thriving. This process is called fostering. A wild mother raises pups born elsewhere as part of her own litter. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild add new genes to a very small population. Genetic diversity helps a population stay healthy. It improves disease resistance and reduces the harm of inbreeding, which happens when close relatives breed. Timing is the biggest challenge. A foster must happen within the first 14 days of a pup’s life. That is when wolf mothers bond with their young and are most likely to accept new pups. Two groups share the work behind American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild. FWS monitors breeding among wild wolves. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) Program guides breeding among wolves in zoos. When a wild litter is born, SAFE looks for zoo-born pups within that narrow window. In 2026, the Saint Louis Zoo’s litter was the only one born in professional care. Partnerships between zoos and wildlife biologists make American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild possible and bring new genes to a very small population. Photo courtesy of Saint Louis Zoo . Professional care means wolves living in zoos and similar facilities. These American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild were the only eligible pups in North America. Regina Mossotti leads the SAFE American Red Wolf Program and serves as the zoo’s vice president of animal care. She says every pup counts when fewer than 40 wolves remain. She sees fostering as a key way to give these pups a chance to support the species’ future. Emily Weller coordinates the FWS Red Wolf Recovery Program. She says several recovery actions rely on close teamwork with SAFE. The American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show how zoo partnerships directly help wild wolves. The wild mother had a large litter. The zoo cross-fostered a few of her pups into its litter at the reserve. This swap helps ensure she can care well for each pup. The exchange also moves genes between wild wolves and zoo wolves. Experts call that a rare and valuable chance for species recovery. The reserve covers 355 acres, roughly 270 football fields, and is closed to visitors. Wolves there learn survival skills with minimal human contact, preparing them for a possible life in the wild. In 2021, the zoo announced plans to develop about 20 acres for wolf conservation. Today, the reserve holds seven habitats for breeding and conservation. The zoo will share photo and video updates on its social media pages and website. Federal biologists continue to support the wild population through the national red wolf recovery effort. Each of the American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild strengthens a population found in only one region. Other reintroduction projects show similar promise, such as efforts to return gray wolves in Colorado . Careful releases and strong partnerships can help wildlife recover. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show what shared effort can achieve. Zoo staff, federal biologists, and a wild mother each played a role. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If your For You Page has been full of people canceling Botox appointments because they started eating more salmon, you’ve found the “eat your skincare” trend. The premise is that the right diet can do what a medicine cabinet full of serums promises. It is, honestly, an appealing one… but it’s also only partly true. The route food takes to your skin When you eat, nutrients get absorbed in the GI tract and travel through the bloodstream to wherever your body decides to send them. There’s no targeting involved, so your skin gets what’s available once everything else takes its share. Topical skincare works on a different logic entirely, putting concentrated ingredients directly on one spot without the detour. “Wrinkles and collagen loss are multifactorial,” says Dr. Kseniya Kobets , Director of Cosmetic Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. “No single food or supplement is going to make a huge difference if the rest of your diet is poor, you are unhealthy or dealing with inflammation, excessive sun exposure or you don’t have a good skincare regimen.” Food can correct deficiencies that slow things down. Vitamin C and amino acids matter for collagen formation; fatty acids support the skin barrier. But more doesn’t mean more. “I think of it as filling the tank,” Dr. Kobets says. “You need the nutrients and building blocks, but overfilling it doesn’t make the collagen-making machinery work faster.” Too much vitamin C, she notes, can cause GI problems and, in some people, raise the risk of kidney stones. Can food protect you from the sun? Some of the content goes further: eat your sunscreen . That sounds ridiculous, but there’s real science underneath it. “There is interesting evidence around oral photoprotection ,” Dr. Kobets says. “Certain carotenoids, polyphenols and Polypodium leucotomos extract have been studied for increasing the skin’s resistance to UV-induced damage.” That’s not a reason to put the SPF away, though. “I sometimes think of these as an extra layer of defense, but definitely not an oral sunscreen,” she says. “No amount of blueberries, green tea or antioxidant supplements is going to replace properly applied and reapplied sunscreen, protective clothing and smart sun behavior.” What to eat for skin health If you want your diet to pull some weight here, the list is manageable. Dr. Sapna Palep , a dermatologist at Journelle Skin, recommends eggs, avocado, flaxseeds, walnuts, salmon, and dark chocolate, which between them cover protein, healthy fats, omega-3 fatty acids , and antioxidants. “Nutrition can influence inflammation, oxidative stress, the microbiome and skin-barrier function,” says Dr. Kobets. “What is good for your overall metabolic health tends to be good for your skin as well.” That’s the version of this trend that holds up: eating well really does support your skin, and the foods involved are things most of us would benefit from eating more of anyway. What food can’t do is replace sunscreen or stand in for a routine that’s doing something. Think of it as filling a role, not playing every position. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM History was made in governors’ races across the country on November 3. In ten states, voters chose candidates who had never held that office before as a matter of historical record, not just political preference: a Black woman elected to the governorship for the first time anywhere in the United States, the first Native American woman to lead any state, the first Latina governor of Texas, the first elected Latino governor of California, the first Black governors of Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin, and the first women ever to win governor’s races in Tennessee, Minnesota, and Ohio. The wins came from both parties and from states that historically appeared to share very little common ground politically, which is part of what made the night so hard to categorize. Georgia elects the first Black woman governor in U.S. history The result that will end up in history books is from Georgia, where Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s race to become the first Black woman ever elected governor of any U.S. state. The country had never crossed this threshold before, not in 250 years of gubernatorial elections. Lance Bottoms is 56 and served as mayor of Atlanta from 2018 to 2022 before moving to Washington as an adviser to former President Joe Biden. Her defeat of Republican health care executive Rick Jackson also makes her the first Democrat to win a Georgia governor’s race in more than two decades, in a state that has been in political motion since it flipped in the 2020 presidential race. New Mexico’s Deb Haaland becomes the first Native American woman governor New Mexico voters sent Deb Haaland to the governor’s office, making her the first Native American woman to hold that position in any state. Haaland, who is of Pueblo Indian descent, has been making this kind of history for most of her public career. She was among the first Native American women elected to Congress, and later became the first Native American cabinet secretary when President Biden appointed her as Interior secretary. Her defeat of Republican Gregg Hull is one more memorable and significant accomplishment. Latino firsts in California and Texas California and Texas, the two most populous states in the country, will each have a Latino governor for the first time. In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra , who served as state attorney general before becoming Biden’s Health and Human Services secretary, defeated Republican Steve Hilton to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom. It was not a close race, but it crossed a threshold the state had never crossed despite having one of the largest Latino populations in the country. Texas is the bigger surprise. Democrat Gina Hinojosa , a state representative, defeated incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, one of the country’s most prominent conservative governors and a close ally of President Trump. Hinojosa is now both the first Latina governor of Texas and the first Democrat to hold the office in more than 30 years. Texas has been changing as its Latino population grows, and Tuesday’s result suggested that shift is now showing up at the top of the ballot. Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin each elect their first Black governors Three more states elected their first Black governor on Tuesday, and these wins came from both sides of the aisle. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds, backed by President Trump, defeated Democrat David Jolly to succeed outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds has served in Congress since 2021 and spent two terms in the state legislature before that; he campaigned on affordability and pledged to continue Florida’s conservative direction. In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford , the state’s attorney general, defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo to become the first Black governor of any state west of the Mississippi River. Ford had already been Nevada’s first Black Senate majority leader and its first Black attorney general; he first won a state legislature seat in 2012, after a career that included practicing law and teaching math. Wisconsin’s win went to Democrat David Crowley , a Milwaukee County executive who beat Republican Congressman Tom Tiffany despite being significantly outspent. His path to the general election is a saga in itself: Crowley suspended his primary campaign before rejoining the race, with the backing of outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, after the candidate he had been supporting dropped out. He ran as someone who can work across the aisle, and the result suggested Wisconsin voters believed him. Three more states elect their first women governors Three states that had never sent a woman to the governor’s office did so on Tuesday. In Tennessee, Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn won a race expected to favor her, though by a narrower margin than most anticipated. She focused on immigration, confronting China, and cutting spending, and will become the first woman ever to hold Tennessee’s governorship. In Minnesota, Democrat Amy Klobuchar defeated Republican Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House, and will become the state’s first woman governor when she takes office in January. Ohio produced the night’s biggest upset. Democrat Amy Acton , who served as the state’s chief public health officer during the pandemic, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a race that turned notably rough in its final weeks, with an attack ad against Acton drawing national attention and criticism. She is now Ohio’s first woman governor, its first Jewish governor, and the first Democrat to hold the office in 20 years. What ten firsts in one night adds up to These results don’t necessarily add up to a single story about where the country is heading. Rather, what each of them does share is that the voters who elected them have done something that hadn’t been done before. Whether that came from changing attitudes about representation, the particular strengths of individual candidates, or just the specific dynamics of this incredible moment in the history of the United States of America, an election night this concentrated in firsts is certainly one to be remembered. Η συνταξιούχος κτηνιατρική νοσοκόμα Carole Webb έσωσε τον μικροσκοπικό άνθρωπο, που ονομάστηκε Tom, αφού τον ανακάλυψαν στην άκρη του δρόμου τον Μάρτιο σε ηλικία μόλις 1 ημέρας. Είναι ασαφές…
items.descriptionOriginal: A piglet saved from a potentially much unkinder fate is now living out the story of Babe after being taken in by a compassionate great-grandmother who owns an animal sanctuary in England. Retired veterinary nurse Carole Webb rescued the tiny fellow, dubbed Tom, after he was discovered on the side of the road in March at just 1 day old. It’s unclear how he came to be there, but Webb theorized that a sow may have given birth while being transported, and the piglet fell from the trailer. The person who found him kept him safe overnight before handing him over to her. FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Tom, who was about the size of a kitten at the time, was hand-reared indoors with hot water bottles and heat pads. Six months later, he’s grown into a pampered pig roaming a three-acre field at the Farm Animal Rescue Sanctuary in Stratford-upon-Avon. “Tom is really just like a real-life Babe,” Webb, 82, told SWNS, adding: “He’s really friendly with the chickens, he’s got a lot of chicken and cat friends — really anything that goes in to see him is his friend.” She said he acts more like a pet dog now than a typical pig, following the farm’s humans around and even coming when he’s called by name. He also has his own stuffed animals, loves to play, and enjoys his treats. “He plays around you and loves being near you. He’s got a big fluffy toy pig, and what he likes to do is lay over it,” she noted. “He loves his belly rubs, too — he’s just the friendliest little pig you could meet.” FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Named after Lord of the Rings character Tom Bombadil , Tom now weighs around 330-450 pounds, a big jump from the tiny piglet that could once fit in the palm of Webb’s hand. “He’s a bit boisterous so we don’t mix him with the sheep, but he’s got the run of one of the field,” said Webb. She noted that the sanctuary is home to about 350 animals, including sheep, cats, chickens, and one other pig. “We also feed the pigeons that are free-flying, and we’ve got an aviary that we put them in until they’re well,” she added. “We’ve got quite a collection.” The sanctuary is currently raising money to buy new land so it can continue caring for its animals. Donate here. This article was originally written by Adam Dutton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets. Αυτή η λεπτομέρεια -- ακριβής και επώδυνη -- είναι το σημείο όπου ξεκινά αυτό το δοκίμιο και θέτει όλα όσα ακολουθούν. Ο συγγραφέας Rajeev Balasubramanyam παρακολούθησε τη θλίψη στο δωμάτιο να θάβεται υπό απόσπαση της προσοχής και αποφάσισε κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: At a funeral for a man who never told anyone he was unhappy, the surviving friends sat around a table and talked about computer games. That detail -- precise and painful -- is where this essay begins, and it sets up everything that follows. Writer Rajeev Balasubramanyam watched the grief in the room get buried under distraction and decided something had to change. He called three old friends scattered across Vancouver, London, Brussels, and Berlin, and he proposed the thing none of them had ever done: a men's circle. The rules were simple -- take turns speaking while others listen and no advice-giving. That last rule proved harder than it sounds; as he notes, dispensing solutions is simply "the way that we, as men, were used to talking." What emerged instead was something quieter and more rare: the feeling of being held. Over a year of online circles, a father died, a cancer survivor admitted he wasn't as fine as he'd thought, and a man in grief finally had space to feel it.
