items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing at the same time. Most food banks and soup kitchens see volunteer demand spike around Thanksgiving , sometimes to the point where they have more help than they can use on that one day. If you want your time to count, a little strategy goes a long way. The good news: there are 17 solid options below, and several of them work whether you have four hours, four minutes, or no desire to leave your couch. National organizations with locations near you These programs operate across all 50 states, so wherever you are, there’s likely a chapter close enough to walk in. Feeding America Feeding America runs the largest hunger-relief network in the country. If you want to volunteer at a food bank on Thanksgiving, call ahead first. Holiday demand often fills slots fast, and some locations redirect walk-ins toward future dates when the need is more consistent. Meals on Wheels Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to seniors who can’t get out on their own. The flexibility here is part of the appeal: you can sign up for a single delivery route or build it into a regular habit. The Salvation Army The Salvation Army works across a wide range of needs, from veterans to abuse survivors to people experiencing homelessness. There’s almost always something useful you can do, even on short notice. Operation Turkey Operation Turkey runs a tightly organized four-hour shift from 8 a.m. to noon, packing meals for homeless individuals. If you want a defined commitment with a clear end time, this is a good fit. Feed My Starving Children Feed My Starving Children packs meals at permanent sites in Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, and Texas. It runs on a reservation system, so sign up before the week of. Toys for Tots Toys for Tots runs its drives through December, so Thanksgiving week is peak season. Volunteer slots exist for collection drives, not just drop-offs. Goodwill Goodwill often looks for people who can share a professional skill, not just sort donations. If you have a background in workforce development, finance, or career coaching, that’s where you’d fit in. United Way United Way sponsors a range of community initiatives, including garden planting, literacy programs, and neighborhood projects. What’s available depends on your city, so look up your local chapter. Local options that don’t require a national signup Soup kitchens and community meal programs often run on the same skeleton crew year after year. A call a week ahead is usually all it takes. Animal shelters are another option, especially if you’re better with dogs than crowds. Staff still work on Thanksgiving, and extra hands for walks or socialization are usually welcome. If you’re up for something more active, turkey trots are 5K races held in communities across the country on Thanksgiving morning, with proceeds going to local charities. You walk or run, and the entry fee does the work. The National Park Service also coordinates trail maintenance and cleanup projects throughout the fall. Check the volunteer page for your nearest park. If you can’t leave the house Gift-a-Family Gift-a-Family lets you sponsor a family through their holiday wishlist. The sign-up deadline is November 30, so there’s still time. Homefront America Homefront America directs donations toward grocery and turkey vouchers for military families. Support Our Troops Support Our Troops coordinates handwritten letters to deployed service members. It takes about ten minutes and goes a long way. One thing to know before you go Holiday volunteering is genuinely good, but the reality is that organizations often need year-round help. Of course, showing up once during the holidays could be the gateway to showing up regularly. If you get redirected on Thanksgiving Day because a food bank is at capacity, ask when they need people most. Often the answer is right after the holiday rush! Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving: 17 options for every schedule first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily . Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Using a similar model, in 2014 Nordberg opened the Montana ranch, where not only employees on the spectrum benefit: She designed most of the cabins specifically for neurodivergent guests. Though anyone can appreciate the soothing atmosphere, it’s particularly accommodating for those on the spectrum, who sometimes experience sensory overload. The calmingly simple cabins provide awe-inspiring vistas of the surrounding mountains with little to no sign of human activity. Hardware was selected to close drawers, cabinets and doors with hardly a sound. Walls, furnishings and bedding are muted earth tones and lights have dimmers. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch is run primarily by young autistic people, some of whom also live on the property. The ranch has unparalleled views of the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains. Autistic and other neurodivergent people are often misunderstood and feel out-of-place, experiencing discrimination, social exclusion, bullying and other situations that can lead to low self-esteem. That — and an inexorable need to mask their differences — often results in depression and anxiety. Some studies indicate that people on the spectrum are four times more likely to experience major depression compared with the general population. “Depression, loneliness, lack of confidence, feeling isolated, rejected, and a lack of community and people who care is what Erik’s Ranch is working to minimize and eliminate,” Nordberg said. And it’s working. John Rekedal, 21, lives in Minnesota but just spent his first summer working at the Montana ranch. When he’s home, he works in a large production greenhouse. And though his coworkers there are understanding, he prefers the camaraderie of working with the ranch’s small staff amid the hush of the surrounding mountains. Jacob Thoresen fetches horses from a pasture in preparation for a trail ride. Thoresen has been working for Erik’s Ranch and Retreats for 10 years. Credit: Jodi Hausen “I’m a whole lot more inclined to work outside,” he said. “And I know everyone’s name. It’s more relaxed.” Cornell University autism researcher Leslie Shaw analyzed a national sample of autistic adults who could answer a survey unassisted and found that only about 53 percent were working in 2023. Furthermore, in 2024, people with cognitive disabilities (of which neurodivergence is a subset) were employed at less than half the rate of people without any disability, according to Cornell’s Northeast ADA Center . These low employment rates may be due to neurotypical employers’ lack of experience with and understanding of neurodivergent people leading to misaligned work assignments, confusion and a fraught or untenable work environment. On a recent late summer day in Montana, Jacob Thoresen, 33, was gearing up to lead a small group of guests on a trail ride. He has been working with the nonprofit for 10 years and splits his time between its two locations. In black cowboy hat and jeans, he walked back and forth across the dirt-floored indoor arena to a tack room, gathering saddles and bridles. He saddled horses while other members dutifully scooped and cleaned areas around the animals. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch & Retreats is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. Thoresen had other jobs before coming to Erik’s. He was a baggage handler at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport and worked in retail and manufacturing. He even tried a desk job. “But,” he said with a smile, “that isn’t me.” Thoresen said he’s gained confidence working with Erik’s Ranch & Retreats. “If you would have met me 10 years ago, I would have been, like, I couldn’t be able to do anything independent and be trusted to actually get the work done,” he said. “This place is teaching me how to be independent. In this last year, I’ve grown more.” He still gets support, but staff, recognizing his achievements, have loosened the reins. “I’m having to rely more on myself to work on those independent skills,” he added. Hannah Jacobs (left) helps Zoe Markman put fresh linens on a bed in one of the guest cabins at Erik’s Ranch. Credit: Jodi Hausen When asked what he finds challenging about working at Erik’s Ranch, Thoresen said workdays can be inconsistent. At the Minnesota retreat, he completes the same tasks daily. On the ranch, daily schedules shift and sometimes he gets overwhelmed. “But I can move through it,” he said. “I attribute that to the staff that I work with and just practice. They do a good job of seeing [my overwhelm] and being like, okay. And that helps, you know. I’ve had too many employers in the past that have been like, ‘Oh, you’re not having a good day? Well, just go home.’” Over the years, Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has employed 27 autistic young adults — 19 in the last year. The goal, Nordberg said, is to serve 30 members regularly. The organization is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. John Rekedal helps clean around the horses in the indoor arena before a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen Not far from Erik’s Ranch, Special K Ranch in Columbus, Montana, provides living quarters and jobs in farming, ranching and gardening and contracts with area businesses to employ adults with developmental disabilities. Over in Jackson, Wyoming, Vertical Harvest integrates people with a wide array of disabilities into their operations growing lettuces, microgreens, tomatoes and basil. In a fully accessible greenhouse, Vertical Harvest operates on what’s known as the “Grow Well” model of employment : providing opportunities for workers to pursue passions by creating or placing them in positions that correspond to their strengths and aspirations, their likes and dislikes. In other words, adapting the workplace to the employee rather than the other way around. Although she hadn’t heard of Grow Well, Nordberg embraces its philosophy. It doesn’t always work out as planned, though. “Not everyone wants to learn hospitality,” she said. In fact, one autistic young man told her he wanted to be a “white hat hacker,” using his computer skills for good. But she didn’t have a role that fit his skills and aspirations. In other instances, however, a member’s passions can be integrated into ranch operations. Part-time member Zoe Markman shows off a colorful collection of eggs gathered from the hens in the coop behind her. Credit: Jodi Hausen Zoe Markman, a 21-year-old autistic woman from Bozeman, loves animals — particularly chickens. So when Markman started working part-time at the ranch, Nordberg built a chicken coop and populated it with more than a dozen hens whom Markman gave punny names: Chiquille O’Neal, Princess Layer and Hen Solo. On a recent workday, Markman gathered more than a dozen colorful eggs. Nordberg also helped Erik start a baking business making cookies, brownies, scones and banana bread. Erik is a visual learner and communicator, so Nordberg created a pictorial cookbook with step-by-step instructions. She marked bins of flour, sugar and other ingredients with pictures so Erik can do most of the work independently. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The ranch can currently house five members and has five cabins and the lodge for guests on its expansive property. So Nordberg has room to expand, and she’d like to. But finances and land-use regulations present barriers. It’s expensive running a guest ranch, though the costs are partly covered by guest fees and philanthropy. And area permitting will only allow for seven more cabins. “This will never be a huge operation,” Nordberg said. But she’s gratified knowing there are places for Erik and others like him to live, belong and find meaningful work. items.descriptionOriginal: Sewage is full of organic matter that can be a source of energy. But it also carries harmful chemicals as well as leftover medicines that conventional treatment methods can’t remove easily. Researchers now report a technology that can solve three sewage-related problems at the same time. Their new device uses bacteria in wastewater to generate electricity while breaking down a hard-to-degrade antibiotic and producing a valuable industrial chemical. The team published their results in Journal of Power Sources . There have been plenty of research efforts to harness microbes for treating wastewater while producing renewable energy. The approach uses microbial fuel cells , which are battery-like devices with two electrodes. In microbial fuel cells, bacteria grow on an electrode and devour organic matter , converting chemical energy into electrons, which flow in an external circuit to produce electricity. Then those electrons meet oxygen at the other electrode to create water. Turns out that microbial fuel cells usually generate very small amounts of electricity. “So we asked a different question: What else could those electrons do when they arrive?,” writes the team from hydrogen peroxide instead of water. Hydrogen peroxide is a household chemical used for disinfection and bleaching. It is also used widely in chemical manufacturing. The chemical industry makes it today using an energy- and chemical-intensive process in large plants. To get the right reaction in the microbial fuel cell, the researchers designed a new electrode. They embedded iron and nickel oxides on a flexible carbon fiber cloth. When they heated the cloth in the presence of acetylene at 800°C, a forest of carbon nanofibers grew out of it. “The metal particles rode the growing fibers upward, so every fiber ended with a metal oxide tip,” the researchers say. So the electrode has conductive fibers with a catalytic tip. And bacteria cling to this rough conductive surface and form a thick film. The team used the same electrodes on both side of the fuel cell. When they ran sewage spiked with the antibiotic chloramphenicol through the cell, it removed 99.99% of the drug while producing hydrogen peroxide in two days. “Next, we plan to run it longer, test other drugs, check the toxicity of the breakdown products and link several cells in series to raise the power,” the team writes. “So can dirty water help pay for its own cleanup? Not completely yet. But in two days, our system turned sewage into cleaner water, a useful chemical and a little electricity.” Source : Yashmeen Budania et al. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes Across 3 million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon, protecting forests from disturbance delivered greater biodiversity benefits than restoring already-cleared land, according to new research comparing conservation strategies. Conservation policy has long debated where limited funding should go: preventing deforestation outright, protecting standing forests from degradation, or restoring land already cleared. A study published in Science this September provides the clearest answer yet, using counterfactual scenarios built from observed land-use changes across three million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon’s deforestation frontier. Led by Leonardo S. Miranda of Lancaster University alongside researchers including Joice Ferreira of Embrapa, the team compared three intervention types against what actually happened on the ground. Protecting forests from disturbance, meaning avoiding fire and selective logging within standing forest, reduced biodiversity loss by 68.5% and carbon loss by 46.8% compared with the baseline scenario. Avoiding deforestation entirely mitigated 60.8% of carbon loss and 28.0% of biodiversity loss. Restoration of already-cleared land delivered the smallest gains for both outcomes. These findings challenge a common assumption in conservation funding, where restoration often receives outsized attention and investment despite standing forests requiring protection first. Protecting forests from disturbance proved nearly as effective as preventing deforestation for carbon storage, while substantially outperforming it for biodiversity outcomes, a distinction with direct implications for how governments and conservation organizations allocate resources. Neither single intervention alone reversed losses across the landscape. Combining avoided deforestation with protection from disturbance was necessary to achieve net-positive outcomes, increasing biodiversity by 12% and carbon by 18% above 2010 baseline levels. This combined approach proved essential precisely because deforestation and forest degradation operate through different mechanisms, requiring complementary rather than substitutable responses. Restoration still carries genuine value, particularly in landscapes where deforestation has already progressed extensively. The research team found that restoration delivered meaningful benefits, particularly on properties where much of the original forest cover had already disappeared, suggesting it works best as a complement to protection rather than a replacement. Protecting forests from disturbance addresses threats that often receive less policy attention than outright deforestation. Selective logging removes valuable timber species while leaving forest canopy nominally intact, and wildfires increasingly penetrate forest edges weakened by fragmentation and drought. Both processes degrade forest structure, reduce habitat quality for forest-dependent species, and release stored carbon, yet they generate far less public attention than visible clear-cutting. Protecting forests from disturbance targets fire and selective logging, threats that degrade forest structure without clear-cutting, with researchers finding that combined deforestation and disturbance avoidance are necessary to achieve net-positive biodiversity and carbon outcomes above 2010 baseline levels. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The study’s timing is especially urgent as climate change intensifies. The research team noted that combined interventions become increasingly important as warming progresses, since forest restoration efforts prove particularly vulnerable to wildfire risk. Newly planted or naturally regenerating young forests lack the structural resilience of mature canopies, making restoration investments vulnerable to being undone by the same fire disturbances the study identifies as critical to prevent. This vulnerability creates a policy challenge extending well beyond Brazil. As governments and international organizations increasingly emphasize forest restoration within climate commitments and biodiversity frameworks, protecting forests from disturbance offers a complementary message: restoration investments achieve far less impact when the remaining standing forest around them continues degrading from fire and logging. Joice Ferreira, principal investigator of the Capoeira restoration research program at Embrapa, emphasized that restoration remains essential precisely where forests have been lost across large areas, reinforcing that the study’s findings don’t diminish restoration’s role but rather clarify where and when it delivers the strongest returns. Restoration works best as part of integrated strategies rather than as a primary tool used independently of forest protection efforts. The research methodology itself offers a template for conservation planning elsewhere. By using observed land-use changes to construct counterfactual scenarios, the team measured what would have happened under different intervention choices and quantified trade-offs that previous studies could only estimate qualitatively. This approach allows policymakers to weigh cost-effectiveness directly rather than relying on intuition about which conservation strategy delivers the greatest return per dollar invested. As tropical deforestation frontiers worldwide face similar pressures from fire, logging, and agricultural expansion, protecting forests from disturbance provides an evidence-based framework extending beyond the Brazilian Amazon alone. The findings suggest that conservation funding achieves maximum impact not through any single strategy in isolation, but through carefully sequenced combinations addressing deforestation, degradation, and restoration simultaneously, each targeting the specific threats most relevant to a given landscape’s current condition. The post Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Το peepal, το banyan, το guular -- thre…
items.descriptionOriginal: For centuries, the sacred groves of Rajasthan were understood as human gifts to nature -- places where belief drew a boundary and the forest was allowed to breathe. But as this essay quietly argues, the order of that story is wrong: people protected a handful of fig trees, and the birds did everything else. The peepal, the banyan, the gular -- three figs that tradition placed beyond the reach of the axe - fed birds through every lean season, and those birds, carrying seeds from across the landscape, built the grove outward from that protected center, generation after generation. "What belief really preserved was a process," the author writes, "a place where the planting could go on undisturbed for centuries." There is something worth sitting with in that realization: that the deepest acts of protection are often for something we cannot fully see, and that what looks like a tree standing alone is, if the birds still come, a forest in the making.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province Reading Time: 3 minutes Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique has officially begun in Nampula Province, aiming to restore 500 hectares of Miombo woodland and build local livelihoods. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique took a major step forward this August with the official launch of a new project in Nampula Province. The initiative pairs the Mozambican government with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), funded by Swiss Development Cooperation. Its goal is to turn national restoration pledges into work that communities can see on the ground. The launch unfolded over two days in Ribáuè District, starting with a briefing for provincial officials and continuing with a public ceremony. Government representatives, private companies, researchers, and local residents participated. Seedlings planted during the event were handed over to a nearby school, where students will track their growth. IUCN’s country representative in Mozambique described the project as reaching well beyond tree planting. The effort aims to improve land productivity and strengthen household livelihoods alongside ecological recovery. That framing positions forest landscape restoration in Mozambique as much an economic strategy as an environmental one. Over the next four years, the project will focus restoration work on 500 hectares within Ribáuè District. Of that total, 400 hectares will restore Miombo woodland, while the remaining 100 hectares will support agroforestry systems mixing crops with trees. The work contributes to Mozambique’s broader Five-Year Programme target of restoring 52,000 hectares nationwide. That national target also feeds into Mozambique’s international commitments under global restoration initiatives. Countries across Africa have pledged millions of hectares to these efforts over the past decade, though turning pledges into on-the-ground results has often proven difficult. A dedicated project with clear hectare targets and funding attached is meant to help close that gap. Miombo woodland stretches across a huge swath of south-central Africa, from Angola to Tanzania and across much of Mozambique. The ecosystem stores significant amounts of carbon and supports roughly half of Africa’s remaining elephant population. Millions of rural households also depend on it directly for firewood, food, and building materials. That dependence cuts both ways. Wood fuel accounts for a large share of household energy use across the Miombo region, which keeps pressure on the woodland high even where restoration work is underway. Providing communities with alternative income sources, rather than relying solely on wood and charcoal, is central to keeping any restored area intact over the long term. Alongside the restoration targets, the project will establish three plant nurseries to supply seedlings for ongoing work. Planners also intend to develop beekeeping and support sustainable value chains tied to cashew, bamboo, and legally harvested timber. Those activities aim to give residents income tied directly to keeping the landscape intact, a key piece of how forest landscape restoration in Mozambique is meant to work in practice. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique ties livelihood directly to conservation, with three community nurseries, beekeeping, and sustainable value chains for cashew, bamboo, and timber giving Nampula residents concrete economic reasons to keep the landscape intact. Photo courtesy of IUCN . Mozambique’s project forms part of a larger global effort known as the FLR Hub, implemented by IUCN alongside other international partners. The hub originally supported restoration work across six countries in Africa and Latin America. A new contribution from Switzerland, announced in late 2025, extended that reach to Mozambique, bringing the total to seven participating countries. According to IUCN, the hub aims to shift restoration efforts from scattered, one-off projects to coordinated approaches that attract long-term investment. That shift matters for a landscape as large and fragmented as the Miombo, where piecemeal efforts have struggled to keep pace with ongoing degradation. Implementation in Ribáuè will rely on continued collaboration between government agencies, private businesses, universities, and civil society groups. Success will depend on whether restored land can deliver real income for residents, not just healthier soil and more trees. Four years is a short window to prove that the model works, but it gives the project a clear point at which results can be measured against the hectare targets set at launch. If it works, forest landscape restoration in Mozambique could offer a model other Miombo countries draw on as they pursue their own restoration commitments. The post Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΑΙΣΙΟΔΟΞΟΥ Μια νέα θεραπεία που εγκρίθηκε από τον FDA για το PTSD ανέφερε ύφεση 68 τοις εκατό σε κλινικές δοκιμές. Τα εγκεκριμένα φάρμακα με την καλύτερη απόδοση για την πάθηση ξεπερνούν περίπου το 10,9%. Η θεραπεία, που ονομάζεται Μαγνητική e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), αναπτύχθηκε από την Wave Neuroscience με έδρα την Καλιφόρνια σε συνεργασία με…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent. The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology. It pairs brain activity mapping with personalized magnetic stimulation. The clinical trial also reported a 52 percent reduction in PTSD symptoms overall. “Our FDA trial reported a 52 percent reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” said Erik Won, D.O., Wave Neuroscience’s chief medical officer. “And more importantly, we saw 68 percent remission in our clinical trial. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.” These results come from different studies, not a direct head-to-head comparison, but the gap is hard to ignore. How MeRT personalizes treatment The process starts with an electroencephalogram (EEG) that records each patient’s brain electrical activity. An AI-assisted algorithm uses that data to build a personalized stimulation plan. A coil placed against the scalp then delivers targeted magnetic pulses through transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique already FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression . Standard TMS follows a generalized protocol. MeRT adjusts based on what’s happening in each patient’s brain. Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a precision medicine researcher at Texas A&M Health who helped guide the study, put it this way: standard TMS covers the leak with a tarp; MeRT tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. Participants received five sessions per week over five to six weeks, but improvements appeared to persist after the sessions ended. The first FDA-cleared non-drug option for PTSD PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980 . Since then, treatment has relied on two FDA-approved medications, both SSRIs, and psychotherapy. A 2020 review found medication remission rates reached 10.9 percent at most. MeRT will be the first FDA-cleared non-medication treatment specifically for PTSD. Dr. Israel Liberzon, the study’s lead psychiatrist and a distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, explained what that means for patients. “Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” he said. “This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety-provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.” About six percent of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans . In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day. “People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.” Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working on insurance coverage to make the therapy more widely accessible. Won also believes MeRT could eventually be adapted for depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric conditions. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Personalized brain therapy hits 68 percent remission for PTSD first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Ο όρος αργκό που είναι δημοφιλής μεταξύ των Gen Z και Gen Alpha ορίζεται ως η καλύτερη απόδοση ή η καλύτερη απόδοση σε κάποιον ή κάτι. Πίστεψε…
items.descriptionOriginal: “Vibe coding,” is so last year. If you want to (try) to get on the same wavelength as teens and tweens, here’s another expression to add to your repertoire: Collins Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year. The slang term popular among Gen Z and Gen Alpha is defined as outperforming or outshining someone or something. Believed to be a shortened version of AMOG (alpha male of the group), the word traces back to bodybuilding culture around the 2010s. But it’s soared in popularity over the past year, with younger generations using it in a more playful way. Collins noted that experts found a 210% increase in usage of the “fast-growing slang word” in 2026, meriting the “word of the year” crown. So how do you use it? If your friend looks amazing in the selfie you just took, but your eyes are closed and hair is out of place — they’re mogging you. Or, to offer a more meta example, mogging is mogging the other words in the dictionary. Other words on the British dictionary’s shortlist include: Bixie : a haircut that’s shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut Fricy : a blend of fruity and spicy Friendslop : a low-budget, independently made video game designed to be played casually with friends Carspreading : the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider, and heavier Hydration break : a pause in a sporting contest to allow the contestants to drink fluids, especially in high heat Ghost job : a role advertised by an employer who has no intention of actually hiring anyone On Oct. 25, Dictionary.com announced its own word of the year: “Maxxing,” a shortened version of “maximizing” that can be used on its own or tacked on to the end of another word to describe the act of optimizing something. Derived from gamer lingo and in use for over a decade, the slang term broke through on TikTok in the 2020s. Its most famous usage is perhaps “looksmaxxing,” which refers to taking a person’s appearance to its full potential, but “sleepmaxxing,” “cozymaxxing,” and “booksmaxxing” have all joined the zeitgeist as well. “Really, anything in your life can get the maxxing treatment, if you do it wholeheartedly enough,” the online dictionary wrote in a blog post.

items.descriptionOriginal: P undits are describing last night as a romp for Democrats, a rebuke of Republicans, a blue tsunami, a rout in the red states. But underneath these headlines is a quieter, parallel story about voters choosing to abandon tribal allegiance and make decisions for themselves. For months, we’ve been hearing about the possibility of a blue wave — and then, in the same breath, the caveat: Is a wave even possible in today’s hyper-polarized America? And yet, in Texas, Florida, Kansas and beyond, the electorate refused to let party loyalty make their choice for them. Young, Latino and red-state voters moved, sometimes dramatically, in just two years. The composition of the two sides turned out to be less fixed than we imagined, with a meaningful number of voters willing to cast ballots across party lines when a candidate, issue or circumstance spoke to them. In Texas, where Democrats had historic wins, people of all parties have recently united to fight against a border wall through Big Bend National Park. Credit: Sam Karas Part of the story was turnout, said New York Times Chief Political Analyst Nate Cohn on The Daily . But, he added, “Many people who are registered as Republicans and voted for Donald Trump voted for the Democratic candidate.” This feels like a fitting conclusion to The Depolarization Project , our special series about how political polarization works and what we can do about it. The premise of that series was that depolarization isn’t about meeting in the middle. It’s about choosing to remain open and curious, rather than blindly clinging to arbitrary affiliations. In the end, many voters showed that their party label doesn’t have the final say. Data center opposition is proving to be a bipartisan, or even nonpartisan, issue across the U.S. Credit: Here Now / Shutterstock Wednesdays are normally “What We’re Reading” day here at Reasons to be Cheerful, so in that spirit, here’s a post-Election Day list of stories from our own depolarization series and from elsewhere around the web. We Hate to Break It to You, But Maybe We’re Not That Polarized – the New York Times A Wall Meant to Divide Is Uniting Left and Right in Texas – Reasons to be Cheerful Voters Vastly Underestimate the Open-Mindedness of Their Political Rivals – PsyPost The Door-to-Door Technique That Actually Changes Minds — Reasons to be Cheerful The post The Election That Transcended Tribalism appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot Reading Time: 3 minutes The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot There’s a moment on most city breaks when you realise you’ve spent more time getting between places than actually enjoying them. You’ve waited for a taxi, sat in traffic, arrived somewhere only to discover it’s a ten-minute walk from where you were half an hour ago. It’s enough to make you wonder why you bothered with the car in the first place. Philadelphia is a city where I’d be inclined to leave it behind.Not everywhere is within walking distance, obviously, but a surprising amount of the central area is. The streets are laid out in a fairly straightforward grid, and there’s plenty to see without travelling particularly far. I’d probably start somewhere around Independence Hall, partly because it’s one of those places you feel you ought to visit, and partly because the surrounding streets are worth a look in their own right. From there, Reading Terminal Market isn’t too far away. I wouldn’t bother making elaborate lunch plans. With that many food stalls under one roof, you’re almost certain to find something you fancy, although deciding what to eat might take longer than expected. Afterward, you could head towards Rittenhouse Square. I rather like the idea of a park that doesn’t try too hard to be an attraction. Rittenhouse is simply a pleasant place to sit for a while, with trees, benches and people going about their day. Somebody’s reading a book. Somebody else is walking a dog that clearly has no intention of going home yet. Meanwhile, the surrounding streets are full of shops, restaurants and apartments. It feels like a proper part of the neighbourhood rather than somewhere created exclusively for visitors. Philadelphia has quite a few green spaces like that, although some are much smaller. Community gardens are particularly interesting. You might find one occupying what was once an empty lot, with vegetables growing in raised beds and a few chairs tucked into a corner. They aren’t necessarily places you’d travel across the city to visit. But coming across one while walking through a residential neighbourhood is rather lovely. And they tell you something about the people who live there. I’d also make time for South Philadelphia. East Passyunk Avenue has the sort of mixture I enjoy: independent shops, restaurants, cafés and ordinary residential streets just around the corner. You can wander without feeling you’re missing some major attraction because you haven’t followed a particular route. The nearby Italian Market area is worth including too, especially if you like looking around food shops. I’d probably end up buying something completely impractical to carry around for the rest of the afternoon. One thing I wouldn’t do is try to squeeze all of Philadelphia into a single walking itinerary. It’s a sizeable city, and there’s no prize for finishing your holiday with sore feet. SEPTA’s buses, trolleys and trains make it possible to cover longer distances without needing a car, which is useful if you want to explore beyond the central neighbourhoods. Where you stay can make the whole thing easier or considerably more annoying. I once heard somebody describe a hotel as being ‘only twenty minutes from everything’, which sounds wonderful until you realise they meant twenty minutes by car. For a trip focused on walking, I’d be looking at the actual streets around the accommodation. Is there somewhere nearby for breakfast? Can you reach a park without crossing several major roads? How far is the nearest transit stop? Those details matter more to me than whether the apartment has an especially impressive television. One of the most effective ways to practice eco-friendly travel is reducing reliance on automobiles during city visits. Philadelphia’s grid layout makes it one of the most pedestrian- and transit-friendly cities in North America, allowing visitors to walk from historic landmarks to local farmers’ markets with ease. Choosing a neighborhood rental situated near public transportation hubs and neighborhood parks allows travelers to experience authentic community life while keeping emissions low. Rather than juggling multiple booking platforms, smart travelers use independent meta-search portals to find well-located accommodations. Exploring Philadelphia vacation rentals via cozycozy gives travelers real-time access to available townhomes, lofts, and historic suites across every major rental portal, making it effortless to lock in a sustainable home base. I’d check the final booking details separately, particularly the exact location and any additional charges. Of course, there’s an environmental benefit to doing more of a city break on foot. Fewer car journeys generally mean fewer transport emissions , and using public transport for longer trips can help reduce your reliance on taxis or a hire car. But I wouldn’t spend the whole weekend thinking about my carbon footprint.I’d be thinking about where to get another coffee, whether there’s time to explore one more street and why I hadn’t left myself longer at the market. That’s probably what makes walking such a good way to experience Philadelphia. You get to see the famous buildings, but you also spend time in the places between them. The little gardens, the corner shops, the streets where nothing especially remarkable is happening.And sometimes those are the bits you remember most. items.descriptionOriginal: As more of the planet’s wild places are consumed by human sprawl, people are increasingly trying to protect wildlife by moving it out of harm’s way. While such relocations might help a construction project clear a regulatory hurdle, it’s often not doing much good for the wildlife, according to new research. Just 6% of amphibian and reptile relocations tied to development could be classified as successful, according to a review of such projects published recently in Conservation Biology . “Moving these species away from a construction site does not mean they will survive in their new home,” said Megan Winand , a University of British Columbia biologist and the lead author. The results offer a sobering look at the performance of this increasingly popular strategy, as development of everything from pipelines to parks clashes with species protections. And while the authors found evidence of ways to improve the performance of such transplant projects, the main takeaway is that it’s usually better to avoid destroying a wild animal’s home than moving the creature to a new one. “We need to prioritize protecting habitat and explore alternatives to current mitigation practices, which this review shows are often failing to achieve meaningful conservation outcomes,” said Winand. The scale of the issue is staggering. While there is no comprehensive count of how often critters are moved to make way for development, a separate 2026 study by many of the same authors found that in British Columbia alone, some 5.1 million amphibians and reptiles were moved just between 2019 and 2022. both;} Recommended Reading: As the world warms, butterflies are relocating at an astonishing scale The new study focuses on cases from around the world where at least something is known about how the transplanted animals fared. They scanned the scientific literature for papers published between 2007 and 2023 that examined the fate of relocated amphibians and reptiles. All told, they looked at 256 case studies tracking everything from tortoises to alligators. Most of the research was concentrated in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand. Nearly 70% of the translocations were done for conservation purposes, such as releasing an animal into habitat that it once occupied. The rest were cases involving animals moved to get them out of the way of development. The researchers then graded a relocation’s performance based on a four-tiered system. The first level was when the original transplants were surviving. A project reached level two when those survivors were reproducing. The third level came when the population was growing. The final, highest level was if a paper showed evidence that the population had achieved longterm viability. Based on that grading system, development-related relocations earned an abysmal grade. Just 6% of the cases were shown to have reached the third or fourth benchmarks. Nearly half of them failed to hit even the first level – that the original population had survived the move. While conservation-related transplants performed more than three times better, that still meant they only reached the top two levels 19% of the time. They had total failures in nearly a quarter of cases. A closer look at the different studies revealed two factors that seemed to contribute to the greater success of the conservation transplants, the scientists found. Things turned out better in cases where people tried to removed threats to an animal in the place where it was being relocated. Higher scores were also linked to more long-term monitoring after the move. “Without adequate follow-up, we won’t know whether animals survive in their new location, reproduce or establish a population that can survive over time,” says Winand. “Relocated animals may also leave the release sites, encounter new threats or face difficult habitat conditions.” So there are things people can do to increase the odds that the transplants will endure. The high failure rate of even the conservation-related measures shouldn’t be taken as a sign of poor execution by the people involved, the authors note. Rather, it illustrates how hard it is to do such translocations, especially for long-lived species that reproduce slowly. It also reinforces a common insight into biodiversity-related work: It’s a lot easier to avoid breaking something in the first place than to try to fix damage later. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Vietnamese Farmers Built a Rice Straw Circular Economy that Pays Reading Time: 3 minutes A rice straw circular economy in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta turns leftover stalks into mushrooms and compost. Rice straw circular economy models give Vietnamese farmers a reason to stop burning their fields. At New Green Farm Cooperative in the Mekong Delta, leftover stalks now feed mushroom beds and compost piles. As a result, member farmers have cut their use of chemical nitrogen fertilizer by 40%. The cooperative works with about 100 farming households across 148 hectares. In its operating area, straw burning has dropped by 90-95%. Farmers are earning more while their fields send up far less smoke. Burning has long been the default after harvest. It clears fields quickly and costs nothing up front. It also fills the air with smoke and dust and releases planet-warming gases. A circular economy offers another path. It keeps materials in use, so one process’s waste becomes the next one’s raw material. In a rice straw circular economy, the stalks become food, fertilizer, and income. New Green Farm put this idea to work in 2023, starting with seven core members. Director Dong Van Canh partnered with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) through the RiceEco project. The Mekong-Republic of Korea Cooperation Fund pays for RiceEco, which supports Vietnam’s One Million Hectares program for low-emission rice. After harvest, a local machinery company bales the straw with mechanized equipment. The cooperative grows mushrooms on about 9,000 bales a year, or roughly 25 a day. Straw also goes into compost, which returns nutrients to the rice fields. That compost explains the drop in chemical fertilizer. Using less fertilizer saves farmers USD 57 to 65 per hectare each season. Selling their straw adds another USD 13 to 15 per hectare per crop. For the cooperative, each mushroom bale earns about 38 US cents in profit, or roughly USD 3,400 a year. Compost adds about USD 2,700 a year, or USD 38 per ton for 72 tons. Canh says the model gives farmers more than one way to earn. Rice still brings in about 60% of the cooperative’s income, while mushrooms add about 30%. Compost, vegetables, and other products make up the rest. In a rice straw circular economy, farmers grow more than rice and cultivate new income sources. Rice provides about 60% of the cooperative’s earnings, while mushrooms contribute another 30%, with compost, vegetables, and other products filling out the rest. Photo by Petr Ganaj on Pexels. That income mix has helped the business grow. Operating space has expanded from 2,500 to about 11,000 square meters, roughly two American football fields. Products now reach buyers in Ho Chi Minh City and on Phu Quoc Island. Canh’s role has changed over time. He moved from field labor to organizing production, managing staff, and finding buyers. His wife runs the cooperative’s onion and chili pepper plots. Other cooperatives in the delta are seeing similar results. In Can Tho, the Tien Thuan Agricultural and Service Cooperative received straw balers and composting machines in June 2024. By September 2025, it was producing 12 to 15 tons of organic fertilizer a month. Circular methods there add USD 50 to 70 of value per hectare. Burning straw or selling it loose adds only about USD 25. The cooperative’s mushroom houses produce up to 1,050 kilograms every six weeks. Farmers there report that field crabs and earthworms have returned, both signs of healthier soil. The work has also created new jobs, especially for women. Machines now handle much of the heavy labor of clearing fields. An estimated 30 to 40% of nearby farmers have adopted similar methods. That uptake matters, because a rice straw circular economy depends on many farms supplying straw. The approach also works outside the delta. In northern Ninh Binh Province, the Nam Cuong cooperative composts rice straw with cow manure for its potatoes. A mechanized turner has cut composting time from 90 days to 45. Potato fields that received this compost yielded 19 to 28 tons per hectare. Plots without it needed 20% more potassium and nitrogen fertilizer. The cooperative now supplies organic produce to meal programs at 20 local schools. Growth has exposed some weak points. New Green Farm faces cash-flow gaps between harvests and limited capital to expand. Storage space also runs short during peak seasons. Affordable loans and better baling equipment would help close those gaps. The cooperative plans larger warehouses for straw collection. Project partners also aim to bring the model to other cooperatives. RiceEco has already brought the rice straw circular economy to 5,084 farmers and other stakeholders. It supports four pilot businesses in Vietnam and Cambodia. Its work also informed Vietnam’s 2023 national guideline on sustainable rice straw management. For generations, people saw straw as something to get rid of. Cooperatives like New Green Farm have turned it into mushrooms, compost, and steady income. The rice straw circular economy shows that the answer to field burning can also be a business plan. The post How Vietnamese Farmers Built a Rice Straw Circular Economy that Pays appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News From Climate Disasters to Resilient Cities: Connecting Technology, Nature, and Communities Reading Time: 3 minutes From Texas floods to Himalayan glacier collapse, cities built for a climate that no longer exists are discovering that real resilience means connecting technology, nature, and people, not just adding more sensors. Before dawn on July 4, 2025, the Guadalupe River at Kerrville rose from about 3 feet to 30 feet in just 45 minutes, turning part of the Texas Hill Country into a disaster zone. In August 2026, a glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border triggered catastrophic flooding that damaged settlements, roads and hydropower infrastructure. Toronto and Southern Ontario have faced their own warning signs. In July 2024, intense rainfall flooded highways and subway stations, while a major power outage affected nearly 300,000 customers. Canada’s 2026 wildfire season has also forced evacuations. These events are geographically different, but they expose a common vulnerability: many cities were built for a climate that no longer exists. Infrastructure designed around historical weather conditions is increasingly being tested by more intense rainfall, extreme heat, wildfires and other climate hazards. We are also pushing against planetary limits. The pressure is broader than climate change alone. The 2025 Planetary Health Check found that seven of the nine planetary boundaries have been crossed, including climate change, freshwater change, biosphere integrity, and ocean acidification. These pressures interact. Damage to ecosystems can weaken carbon sinks, while climate change can disrupt freshwater cycles. In 2026, the United Nations University warned of “global water bankruptcy,” describing water systems so depleted or degraded that they may no longer easily return to historical conditions. For cities, these pressures quickly become infrastructure challenges. Extreme rainfall overwhelms stormwater systems. Heat stresses buildings, electricity grids and public health. Drought and groundwater depletion threaten water security. This is why mitigation and adaptation cannot be treated as separate agendas. Mitigation reduces the emissions driving future warming. Adaptation reduces impacts that are already occurring or can no longer be fully avoided. Yet adaptation has a major financing problem. UNEP estimates that developing countries will need about US$310 billion to US$365 billion annually by 2035, while international public adaptation finance flows were only US$26 billion in 2023. Adaptation needs are now roughly 12 to 14 times current flows. Resilience plans cannot remain on paper when cities need drainage, cooling, early-warning and water systems now. What does a climate-resilient city actually look like? Smart buildings can reduce energy demand through efficient design, sensors and automated controls while improving thermal comfort and indoor air quality. At the neighbourhood scale, renewables, storage, microgrids and electric mobility can reduce emissions while strengthening resilience. Internet of Things, or IoT, technologies can monitor rainfall, drainage, temperature and infrastructure performance. But a community is not “smart” simply because it has more sensors. Some of the most powerful solutions work with natural systems. Low-impact development and sustainable stormwater management use rain gardens, bioswales, permeable pavements, green roofs, infiltration areas, and rainwater harvesting to retain, absorb, filter, or reuse rainfall close to where it falls. Blue-green infrastructure extends this through wetlands, urban forests, ponds, and waterways. The principle is simple: instead of designing cities only to move water away as quickly as possible, we can design them to absorb, store, filter, and reuse it. Blue-green infrastructure shifts urban water management from moving rainfall away as fast as possible to absorbing, storing, filtering, and reusing it through rain gardens, bioswales, wetlands, green roofs, and urban forests built into the city fabric. Photo by Shox Art on Pexels. Bangladesh offers a powerful community-level example. In salinity-affected coastal areas, women trained as “Pani Apas,” or water sisters, help households use and maintain rainwater-harvesting systems. The model does more than provide water tanks. It connects climate adaptation with safer water, women’s livelihoods, skills and community ownership. UNDP reports that related coastal initiatives provide year-round safe drinking water to nearly 140,000 people in parts of Khulna and Satkhira. Costa Rica offers a different lesson from Latin America. Since 2015, nearly all of its electricity has come from renewable sources, with hydropower supplying around 70%, alongside wind and geothermal power. Yet prolonged dry periods increasingly challenge hydropower production. Costa Rica therefore illustrates why mitigation and adaptation must advance together. A clean electricity system still needs diversified renewables, resilient grids and water-aware planning. The five Ps of sustainable development, People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership, provide a useful way to judge these solutions. People ask who is protected. Planet asks whether emissions, water, and ecosystems are considered together. Prosperity asks whether investment creates livelihoods and resilient infrastructure. Peace brings in fairness, trust and accountable institutions. Partnership recognizes that governments, communities, engineers, businesses and civil society organizations must work together. The major gap today is often not the absence of solutions. It is our failure to connect them, finance them adequately, implement them equitably and maintain them over time. Sensors can warn us that water is rising. Blue-green infrastructure can help absorb it. Rainwater harvesting can turn rainfall into a resource. Clean electricity can reduce emissions. But people still need the knowledge, resources and authority to operate these systems and shape the decisions behind them. A truly smart and resilient city is not the one with the most connected devices. It is the one that connects technology, nature, infrastructure and people well enough to reduce risk before disaster occurs, protect the most vulnerable and recover more equitably when disruption cannot be avoided. The post From Climate Disasters to Resilient Cities: Connecting Technology, Nature, and Communities appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Karl Bushby left Chile on foot in 1998 at age 29, with golden hair and two iron rules: no machines to carry him forward, and no coming home — not for illness, not for grief, not for anything. Twenty-eight years, 75 million steps, one polar bear encounter, 31 days swimming the Caspian Sea, and a jail cell in Panama later, he walked up to his mother's house in Hull, England, pushing the same cart he'd had for a quarter century. The cheers fell quiet at the doorstep. What lingers most isn't the staggering mileage but the strange disorientation of arrival — he found himself looking the wrong way crossing the road in his own country, a foreigner in his birthplace. "I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long," he said. "I almost feel guilt." Nearly half his life spent walking the earth had multiplied his sense of belonging until home meant something far larger and more complicated than a red-brick terrace in northern England. His parting thought wasn't about endurance or willpower — it was a quiet insistence that the world is full of people who have drastically underestimated themselves, and that the first step is simply imagining otherwise.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Upcycling Food Industry Byproducts into Ingredients People Want to Eat Reading Time: 3 minutes Upcycling food industry byproducts turns factory leftovers into tasty, useful ingredients. Dutch company Greencovery shows how this can work for food makers. Upcycling food industry byproducts means turning leftover material from food factories into new ingredients. Food makers often call these leftovers side streams. Many side streams end up discarded or sold as animal feed. Greencovery , a company based in Wageningen in the Netherlands, wants to change that. It says its patented technology recovers valuable ingredients from side streams. The goal is to create new revenue for manufacturers and a lighter footprint on the planet. The scale of food waste is large. The UN Environment Programme reported that the world wasted 1.05 billion metric tons of food in 2022. That equals about 19% of the food available to consumers. Those figures cover homes, restaurants, and stores, not factory leftovers. Still, they show why finding new uses for food matters. Food loss and waste also affect the climate. The same report links it to 8% to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions. That is almost five times the emissions from the aviation sector. A side stream is the material left after a factory makes its main product. That material often still holds useful compounds. Greencovery focuses on pulling those compounds out and returning them to the food supply. Animal feed is a common destination for these leftovers. Greencovery describes it as a lower-value outcome than human food. Its team sees upcycling food industry byproducts as a way to move more material toward food ingredients. The company uses what it calls mild separation technology. Separation means pulling the useful parts out of a mixture. Mild means gentle conditions, and the company says the method uses less energy and water than other separation techniques. Why does that matter? The company says the ingredients it extracts carry a low carbon footprint. A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases released to make a product. The recovered ingredients bring three listed strengths: high functionality, great taste, and microbial stability. Functionality means an ingredient performs well in recipes. Microbial stability means it resists spoilage by microbes and holds up in storage. Upcycling food industry byproducts turns okara, the often-overlooked soy pulp left after soy milk or tofu production, into Okara Pro and Okara Tex, two neutral-tasting, nutritious ingredients suited to bakery goods, savory dishes, and plant-based meat. Photo by Polina Tankilevitch on Pexels. Greencovery does not stop at the lab. It guides partners through three checkpoints for upcycling food industry byproducts. Each one answers a question. Does it work? Does the market want it? Is it commercially viable? The first checkpoint is a proof of concept, which tests whether the idea works technically. The team also runs early product trials to see if a side stream can become a functional ingredient. Next comes a proof of market, which checks whether buyers want the product. The team tests taste, function, and nutrition. It also brings potential buyers into the conversation early. The final step is a proof of business. It covers pricing, costs, profit margins, and supply chains. Greencovery also co-invests with partners and helps set up production in a suitable location. The team blends technology experts, food application specialists, and business experts. Together, they test both the science and the numbers. Two real products show upcycling food industry byproducts at work. The company has made a high-fiber satay sauce and a Parmigiano Reggiano mayonnaise. Both reflect its aim of using ingredients that might otherwise be discarded. The Dutch Prime Minister met the team and experienced both products firsthand. The meeting took place during the Netherlands’ food waste awareness week. Foodvalley NL, a group that promotes innovation and sustainability in food, invited Greencovery to the event. The talks focused on cutting food waste and finding better uses for ingredients. Greencovery also thanked the Upcycling Community for its support. Greencovery says it works to speed up the path from idea to market. Faster launches help companies see returns sooner. Manufacturers curious about their own side streams can start small. Greencovery offers a free 30-minute consultation call. These claims come from Greencovery itself, so readers should treat them as company-reported. Food makers considering upcycling their food byproducts should run their own trials and check local food safety rules before launching a product. Shoppers can play a part too. Choosing upcycled foods signals demand, which encourages more companies to try. Shoppers interested in upcycling food industry byproducts should read labels closely. A product can earn the upcycled label with only 10% upcycled ingredients by weight, so it helps to learn what the upcycled label actually requires. Organic foods, by comparison, must contain at least 95% certified organic ingredients. Food waste remains a large problem, but practical tools to shrink it are taking shape. Upcycling food industry byproducts gives manufacturers a clear path from leftover to ingredient. With testing, market checks, and careful planning, a side stream can become a product people choose to buy. items.descriptionOriginal: Recommendations are independently selected by our team but may result in a commission to Nice News which helps keep our content free. Nice News readers know there’s no shortage of nice things in the world, and that includes products that make our lives a little better and brighter. For 2026, we’ve got an unbeatable hair brush, a cordless vacuum, scented bookmarks, and more. Combined, these 20 products comprise a pretty great holiday shopping guide, if we do say so ourselves. Sure, it’s more expensive than the ones you can grab at a drugstore, but for something I use every day, it’s a major upgrade. My hair feels silky smooth, the bristles navigate knots with ease, and it has that signature sleek Dyson design. Brett, Senior Account Manager: Levoit Cordless Vacuum Cleaner Courtesy of Levoit Shop LEVOIT SHOP AMAZON My cordless vacuum is easily one of my favorite purchases this year. I love how convenient and lightweight it is, making it extremely easy to quickly clean up my everyday messes without having to drag out a bulky vacuum or worry about cords. Turtlebox Original (Gen 3) Speaker Courtesy of Turtlebox Shop TURTLEBOX SHOP AMAZON This Bluetooth speaker has been perfect for everything from backyard parties to beach days, with impressive sound quality and durability that’s truly second to none. The best part is knowing I can bring it anywhere without having to worry about it getting knocked around or damaged. Josh, Content Strategist: Apple Airpods 4 Courtesy of Apple Shop AMAZON The AirPods 4 with active noise cancellation have become my preferred choice for work. Their noise cancellation performs noticeably better than other earbuds I own. I use them to block out background sounds without playing any music, and they’ve significantly boosted my focus and productivity. UGREEN Wireless Mouse 2.4G Courtesy of UGREEN Shop Amazon As someone who dislikes touchpads, this mouse has been a lifesaver. Setup was effortless, it’s super responsive, comfortable, and ergonomic, and the battery life is amazing — I’ve only needed to charge it a few times since March! Marika, Contributing Writer: Solar Rainbow Maker Window Charm Courtesy of Uncommon Goods Shop UNCOMMON GOODS Shop AMAZON ​I’m amazed by this rainbow maker! It hangs on a window in the sunniest nook of our home and scatters rainbows across the kitchen. It’s so magical that even my dog seems to get a kick out of looking at the colors (or maybe watching me get a kick out of them ). Highly recommend scrolling through the customer reviews to see examples of it in action. Violette_FR Bisou Balm Lipstick Courtesy of Violette_FR shop violette_fr SHOP SEPHORA Bisou Balm made me a lipstick person. I love the matte “blush for the lips” look and it smells like a waffle. I have it in Rose Latte and I’m tempted to try the bestseller Bêtise, but I don’t want to mess with a good thing! Thule Sapling Baby Backpack Courtesy of Thule Shop THULE This backpack baby carrier is my favorite thing from my baby registry. It feels so secure and gives me peace of mind knowing my daughter is tucked in and protected from the sun while we hike uphill, downhill, wherever. And she seems to love the view! The bottom compartment is also surprisingly roomy and fits everything we need when we leave the house, which is a lot. Mike, SVP, Editorial Strategy Aftelier Perfumes Biblioscents Scented Bookmarks Courtesy of Aftelier Perfumes Shop AMAZON Shop Aftelier PErfumes If you love to read and were mildly obsessed with scratch-and-sniff stickers as a kid, consider ditching the dog-ears for a four-pack of Biblioscents. Scratching the botanical illustration on each bookmark releases a grown-up scent — ginger root, frankincense, vetiver, geranium — for an adult version of an old habit. Natalie, Senior Managing Editor YQh Retractable Sink Storage Rack Courtesy of YQh Shop AMAZON You know those products you didn’t realize you needed until you discovered they existed? This retractable sink rack is on that list. After having purchased multiple sink caddies that left water pooling by the kitchen faucet, I wanted an organizer that freed up space and didn’t require me to wipe down the countertop every time I washed a dish. This rack is exactly what I was (unknowingly) looking for: It expands over the sink, allowing water from the soap dispenser and sponge to drip directly down the drain. It’s also stainless steel and has a slim design with anti-slip rubber sleeves that help keep it in place. Plank+Beam Contour Console Table Courtesy of Plank + Beam Shop plank + Beam Shop Amazon I’d been on the hunt for a console table for months and fell in love with this one from Plank+Beam as soon as I saw it. It’s constructed of solid pine wood, easy to assemble, and the perfect height and length for my narrow entryway (I got the 56-inch length, but it’s also available in 46 inches). It comes in three wood finishes and looks extremely high-end but sells at a much lower price point than comparable options from well-known furniture stores. Rebekah, Staff Editor: Levi’s Men’s Chino Tech Pants Courtesy of Levi’s Shop AMAZON My husband wanted some casual but elevated pants that he could wear both to the office and out on the town. I’m a big fan of the ones he chose. They have the tiniest bit of sheen and a little give, so they’re comfy while also looking sharp. He just bought two more pairs in blue and khaki. Thrive Causemetics Tubing Mascara Courtesy of Thrive Causemetics Shop Thrive SHOP AMAZON I decided to finally hop on the tubing mascara bandwagon, and Thrive’s was the one I saw most recommended on Reddit. I finally get the hype. The lengthening formula wraps each lash in a lightweight, buildable tube that doesn’t smudge or run. It’s vegan and cruelty-free, comes in multiple colors, and taking it off at night is so much easier than I’m used to with typical waterproof options. Total game changer. Once you get the spray bottle, you only have to purchase the glass bottles of concentrate to refresh your supply. The system makes for a more sustainable way to clean your home, and it smells great! items.descriptionOriginal: Dietary guidelines seem to run the gamut depending on where you live. In Japan, grain-based dishes are the main focus, while Greece promotes the Mediterranean diet and the U.S. emphasizes protein . So nutrition scientists from around the globe recently came together to develop a compendium of advice that’s adaptable across cultures (and takes the health of the planet into account). Enter: the International Food Guide Pyramid. The team compared national and regional dietary guidelines from the United States, Canada, Germany, Australia, China, the Netherlands, and the Nordic countries, in addition to analyzing more than 250 scientific publications, to pinpoint the shared fundamentals of healthy eating. As it turns out, they may be more universal than it often seems. “Despite what people often hear, there’s actually substantial agreement in nutrition science about the foundations of healthy eating,” study lead Karen Della Corte said in a news release. She added that a balanced diet will look different for each person, so the guidelines are designed to be adjusted to include local, affordable, and culturally appropriate foods. The new food pyramid focuses on plant foods, healthier sources of fat and protein, and high-quality carbohydrates. At the base — representing the foundation of a nourishing diet — are vegetables and fruit as well as whole and low-glycemic index grains. Above that are plant-based proteins like beans, nuts, and seeds, as well as plant-based oils. Next up are fish, poultry, eggs, and certain dairy products, and at the top, for use sparingly, are refined grains, red and processed meats, butter, chips, sugary drinks and snacks, and salt. A 2025 report from the EAT-Lancet commission called for similarly plant-forward international guidelines, suggesting they could prevent 15 million premature deaths per year and reduce environmental impacts like greenhouse gas emissions. “Our diet has to be not only for our own health but also for the health of our planet,” said David Jenkins of the University of Toronto, creator of the glycemic index. “Our science base has to be appropriately comprehensive to include that.” Karen Della Corte Corte offered the following advice for putting the pyramid’s principles into practice: Design your meal around the plant food you want to emphasize, first thinking about which vegetables, whole grains, beans, or lentils you could include. Opt for beans, peas, lentils, fish, poultry, or yogurt more frequently than red or processed meats, and don’t make meat the biggest part of any meal. Reach for snacks like nuts, seeds, fruit, or vegetables with hummus over less nutritious processed options. Choose whole-grain bread over refined white bread and whole-grain or high-fiber cereals rather than refined, puffed, flaked, or popped cereals. Use canola or olive oil in your cooking instead of animal fats like butter or tallow. Drink water instead of soda.
